(p-63) (Surat al-Hijr is Meccan, except verse 87, which is Medinan, and its verses number ninety-nine.)

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra.﴾ The discussion of this, and of its place at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd and its counterparts, has already passed.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to it, meaning: those are the verses of this surah, which is of great standing, ﴿of the Book﴾, the complete and well-known Book, which needs no description and is famous above all books as the one deserving that the name "the Book" be applied to it without qualification. That is, some of it is distinguished and set apart by a specific name. It refers either to the whole Qur'an, or to all of what had been revealed up to that time, since that is what comes first to mind when the term is used without qualification. On this reading, the benefit of describing the verses with the attributes of perfection that are attached to them is clear. This is not the case if "the Book" is taken to refer to the surah, since a surah does not have such a degree of fame as to make the explicit description unnecessary, and it is also not the case that it refers to all of its verses. So it is necessary to take "those" as pointing to each one of them individually, and this involves a degree of strain that is not hidden, as was mentioned in Surat al-Ra'd.

﴿And a Qur'an﴾, that is, a Qur'an of great standing, ﴿clear﴾, making manifest what is within its contents of wisdom and rulings, or the path of right guidance and error, or distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. Its great standing has been magnified, with the combination in it of the two attributes of being a Book and being a Qur'an, in two ways:

The first: its inclusion of the attributes of perfection of the genus of divine books, so that it is as if it were all of them. The second: the manner in which it is distinguished from others, unique in its kind, unprecedented in its field, beyond the scope of eloquence. The second manner is placed last because pointing to its distinction from all other books after alerting to its encompassing the perfections of the other books is more effective in praise, lest it be wrongly supposed from the outset that its distinction from others is due merely to its independence with special attributes peculiar to it, without including the attributes of perfection of all the other noble books. The discussion is similar at the opening of Surat al-Naml, except that there the Qur'an is mentioned before the Book, for reasons that will be explained there.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 2:

When he had made clear that this noble surah is a part of the Book, and the Qur'an, to direct the addressees toward receiving well what it contains of rulings, narratives, and admonitions, he began to explain what it includes, so it was said: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾

﴿Rubama﴾ is with a damma on the ra' and a light ba' with a fatha. It has also been read with a shadda, with a fatha on the ra' and light, and with an added ta' with a shadda. It has eight dialects: a fatha or damma on the ra' with a shadda or without, and likewise with an added ta' with a shadda or without. "Rubba" (رُبَّ) is a particle of genitive that enters only upon a noun, and "ma" (ما) is a kafa (restrictive) particle that makes it admissible for it to enter upon a verb. Its proper place is to enter upon the past tense, and its entering upon His words, exalted is He, ﴿those who disbelieved will wish﴾ is because what is expected in His reports, exalted is He, is like the past that is certain in its occurrence. So it is as if it were said: "Perhaps those who disbelieved wished," and what is meant is their disbelief in the Book and the Qur'an, and that it is from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿had they been Muslims﴾, submitting to His judgment and yielding to His command. In this there is an indication that their disbelief was only through denial, after they had known that it is from Allah, exalted is He. That wish will be on the Day of Resurrection, or at their death, or at witnessing their condition and the condition of the Muslims, or at seeing the disobedient Muslims being brought out of the Fire.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes and the people of the Fire have gathered in the Fire, and with them are whomever Allah, exalted is He, wills from the people of the qibla (i.e., Muslims), the disbelievers will say to them: 'Were you not Muslims?' They will say: 'Yes.' They will say: 'Then what did your Islam avail you, when you have become with us in the Fire?' They will say: 'We had sins, and we were seized for them.' Then Allah, glorified is He, will become angry for them by the bounty of His mercy, and He will command that everyone from the people of the qibla who is in the Fire be brought out of it. They will come out of it, and then those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims." 

Mujahid related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The Lord will continue to show mercy, and intercession will be made to Him, until He says: 'Whoever was among the Muslims, let him enter Paradise.' At that point they will wish for Islam."

The truth is that this is to be understood as referring to the intensity of their wish. As for the wish itself, it is not specific to one time rather than another; rather it is established and continuous at every moment that passes over them. The purpose is to explain that, as it is in its abundance. The form of diminution (تقليل) is used in accordance with the custom of the Arabs in what they intend as exaggeration, by way of reversal. You say to one of the commanders of the armies: "How many horsemen do you have?" and he says: "A horseman, perhaps, is with me," or "You will not lack a horseman with me," while he has many companies of cavalry. His intention in that is to deny the claim of increasing his horsemen, but he wants to show his freedom from exaggeration and to make clear that he is one who minimizes what he has out of loftiness of aspiration, let alone increasing what is little. This method is only adopted when the matter is so clear that no shadow of doubt hovers around it, so that one turns to it in order to do justice to the truth. The noble wording thus indicates the disbelievers' wish for Islam at every moment of the Last Day, and that this is so evident that it cannot be confused by anyone, even if a speech were brought that indicated its opposite. It also indicates that this wish, despite its abundance in itself, is considered slight in relation to the majesty of the Lord, and this is what suits the context of explaining the insignificance of the disbelievers' affair and the disregard for what they are in of disbelief and denial, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Leave them to eat﴾ ... the verse expresses.

Or, going toward indicating that it is the nature of the intelligent person that when a matter presents itself which is presumed to be praiseworthy, or which is rarely otherwise, he does not part from it, nor part from its opposite. So how much more so when praise is certain? As in their saying: "Perhaps you will regret what you have done," and "Perhaps a person regrets what he did," for the intention is not to explain that regret is hoped to occur without certainty of it, or that it rarely occurs, but rather to alert that the intelligent person does not engage in what regret is hoped to follow from, or whose occurrence is rare. So how much more so with what is certain to occur? And a little regret suffices to be a barrier from that act, so how much more so with much regret? The purpose of adopting this method is to show elevation and self-sufficiency, without explicitly stating the goal, on the basis that its manifestness is presumed. The meaning is: if they wished for Islam only once, it would be obligatory for them not to part from it. So how much more so when they wish for it at every moment? This is more fitting to the context of bringing them down from what they are upon of disbelief. These two methods are distinct in essence and in context, so whoever thinks them one has failed to give the context its due.

[Dhalika] "Leave them" (dharhum): let them be, i.e., do not keep admonishing them about what they are engaged in, with reminder and counsel, since there is no way to get them to desist from that. Persist in leaving them to themselves and their affairs; indeed, order them to pursue what they are pursuing.

"Let them eat and enjoy themselves" (ya'kulu wa-yatamatta'u): with their worldly life. The placing of eating first indicates that their enjoyment is of the sort of the enjoyment of beasts in food and drink. (p-65) What is meant is their continuation in that, not its initiation, for they were already like that. Or it means their enjoying themselves without hearing what disturbs their living, namely the calamities and the warnings, for enjoyment in that manner is a newly arising matter, and it may be that it is consequent upon leaving them to themselves.

"And let hope distract them" (wa-yulhihim): and let them be occupied, i.e., let them be diverted from following you, or from reflecting on what they are coming to, or from faith and obedience, for eating and enjoyment lead to that. "Hope" (al-amal): the expectation of long lives, attaining aims, the stability of conditions, and that they will meet in the final outcome and the end only good.

The three verbs are in the jussive mood as an answer (al-jawabiyya) to the imperative, as you know from the implication of the command to abandon being a command to them to do these things, by way of metaphor. Or the intended meaning of the listed verbs is that they engage in them heedless of the gravity of their outcome, not hearing at all of the evil of its consequence. There is no doubt that this follows from the command to abandon, since the prohibition of what they are upon of committing abominations would disturb their enjoyment and spoil their living; so he, peace be upon him, was commanded to leave it, so that they would wallow in what they are in of their portions, and what befalls them would overtake them while they are heedless of it.

"Then they will come to know" (fa-sawfa ya'lamun): the evil of their conduct, or the gravity of its outcome, or the reality of the state which compelled them to the aforementioned wishful thinking, since they did not know that from you. This, together with being a threat of the utmost severity and a menace following menace, is a reason for the command to abandon, since their knowing that is a cause for ceasing prohibition and counsel to them. In it is the establishment of proof against them and an exaggeration in warning, since the command to the contrary is not realized except after repeated warning and the firm establishment of denial and rejection. Likewise is what is consequent upon it of eating, enjoyment, and distraction.

*Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 4:*

﴿وَما أهْلَكْنا﴾ [And We did not destroy] begins an explanation of the reason their punishment is delayed until the Day of Resurrection, and of why they are not placed among the nations that hasten toward punishment. That is, ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ [any town] of the towns ﴿بِالخَسْفِ بِها، وبِأهْلِها﴾ [by sinking it, along with its people, as was done to some of them], ﴿أوْ بِإخْلائِها عَنْ أهْلِها غِبَّ إهْلاكِهِمْ﴾ [or by emptying it of its people after their destruction, as was done to others]. ﴿إلا ولَها﴾ [except that it has] ﴿فِي ذَلِكَ الشَّأْنِ﴾ [in that matter] ﴿كِتابٌ﴾ [a decree], that is, a fixed term written in the *al-lawh* (the Preserved Tablet) that must be observed, such that it cannot be changed, since it occurs in accordance with the wisdom that requires it. ﴿مَعْلُومٌ﴾ [known] means it is not forgotten or neglected, so that deviation from it, by advancing or delaying, could be imagined.

So *kitab* (كِتابٌ) is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*), and the whole clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) modifying *qaryah* (قَرْيَةٍ). Because the noun is indefinite and general, and especially since it is emphasized by the word *min* (مِن), it functions as if it were a qualifying clause (*fi hukm al-mawsufah*), as has been indicated. The meaning is: We did not destroy any town of the towns in any state except in the state where it has a decree, that is, a fixed term for its destruction which We have written; We do not destroy it before its appointed time, which is known and not neglected, so that its violation through advancing or delaying would be possible. Alternatively, the clause is read as a predicate, meaning: We did not destroy any town of the towns in any state except that, with regard to its destruction, there was a decree for it, that is, a determined term written in the Tablet, known and not neglected.

Or the clause may be a qualifier (*sifah*), but not of the town mentioned. Rather, it qualifies the indefinite noun that follows *illa* (إلّا) and serves as a substitute (*badal*) for the mentioned noun according to the preferred view. Thus it has the same status as a qualifier of the mentioned noun. The meaning is: We did not destroy any town of the towns except a town for which there is a known decree. This is like the words of Allah the Exalted:

﴿لَيْسَ لَهم طَعامٌ إلا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾ [They shall have no food except from thorny plants] ﴿لا يُسْمِنُ﴾ [which neither nourishes nor relieves hunger].

Here, *la yusminu* (لا يُسْمِنُ) is a qualifier, but not of the food mentioned, because that would only indicate that their food, which does not nourish, is restricted to *dari'* (ضَرِيعٍ, thorny plants). That is not the intended meaning. Rather, it qualifies the food implied after *illa*, meaning: They have no food of any kind except food that does not nourish. Therefore there is no separation between the qualified noun and its qualifier by the word *illa*, as some have supposed. As for placing *waw* (الواو) between them, although the rule is that it should not be there, this indicates the complete closeness of the two, since the function of *waw* is to join and connect. What is under discussion, the qualifier, adheres more closely to the qualified noun than the other way around.

[In Allah's words:] ﴿وَما أهْلَكْنا مِن قَرْيَةٍ إلا لَها مُنْذِرُونَ﴾ [And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners], the impossibility of separating destruction from its fixed term is rational (*'aqli*), while separating it from warning is customary (*'adi*), following the divine way (*al-sunnah al-ilahiyyah*). Since He has explained that each destroyed nation had a specific time for its destruction, and that it happened only as it was written in the Tablet, He then explains that every nation among them, and among others, has a decree that cannot be advanced or delayed.

Then it is said: ﴿No nation can outrun its term, nor can they delay it.﴾

﴿No nation can outrun﴾ from the destroyed nations and others ﴿its term﴾ which is written in its Book; that is, its destruction does not come before the coming of its Book, or no nation passes away before its appointed term passes. For when "outrunning" (al-sabq) relates to a temporal thing, its meaning is surpassing and leaving behind. So when you say, "Zayd outran ʿAmr," its meaning is that he surpassed him and left him behind. But when it relates to a time, the matter is the reverse. The secret in this is that time is considered in terms of movement and orientation toward the speaker, so that what precedes it is realized before its realization. As for the temporal thing, what is considered in it is movement and orientation toward what will come of time. Thus the one who outruns is the one who advances toward the goal. Its mention under the heading of "term" is in consideration of what the term requires of outrunning, just as its mention under the heading of "the known Book" is in consideration of what it necessitates of destruction.

﴿Nor can they delay﴾, that is: nor can they lag behind. The form of the verb (istifʿal) indicates their inability to do so despite their seeking it. The choice of the present form for both verbs after the mention of the negation of destruction in the past form is because the purpose is to explain their continuity and persistence among the past and remaining nations. Attributing these two to the nation after attributing destruction to the town is because outrunning and delaying are the condition of the nation, not of the town, along with the generality of "nation" to the people of those towns and others whose punishments were postponed until the Hereafter. The mention of their not lagging behind is placed after the mention of their not outrunning, even though the context is one of emphasis on the certainty of their punishment, either in consideration of the precedence of outrunning in existence, or in consideration that the purpose is to explain the secret of postponing their punishment despite their deserving it. The verb is given in the masculine plural form to carry the meaning with the masculine taking precedence, and for the sake of the rhyme endings (fawasil). For this reason the prepositional phrase is omitted. The sentence clarifies what preceded, and the meaning is that the postponement of their punishment until the Day of Resurrection is as indicated by the explanation of their wishing for Islam at that time. And the command to leave them and their affairs until they know the reality of the situation is only due to the delay of their appointed term, which is determined by what it requires of perfect wisdoms, among which is what God Most High knows of the faith of some of those who will emerge from them until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And they say﴾: this begins an explanation of their disbelief toward the one to whom the Book was revealed, after the explanation of their disbelief in the Book itself, and of what their state will come to. The speakers are the polytheists of Mecca, owing to the extreme of their obstinacy in rebellion and error. ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾: they addressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with this, not as acceptance of it or belief in it, but as mockery of him, peace and blessings be upon him, and to indicate the basis of their false judgment in their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are surely a madman﴾. This is like the practice of Pharaoh when he said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾. They mean: O you who claim such a wondrous matter that breaks customary norms, indeed you are, on account of that claim, or by the evidence of what befalls you when you claim that it is sent down to you, surely a madman.

(p-67) The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur, "the prepositional phrase") before the substitute for the agent (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il, "the deputy of the agent," i.e., the grammatical subject of the passive verb) is because their denial is directed at the revealed item being a Reminder from God, Exalted is He, and not at the one upon whom it was revealed being the Messenger of God, after granting that what was revealed came from Him, Exalted is He. This is as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾, for there the denial is directed at the one upon whom it was revealed being the Messenger of God, Exalted is He. The verb being stated in the passive form (al-majhul, "the passive") is to give the impression that this is not an act that has an agent, or to direct the denial at the revelation's reaching him rather than at its being attributed to an agent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 7:

﴿Why do you not bring us﴾: the word "law" (lawla, "if only" / "why not") when combined with "ma" conveys what it conveys when combined with "la": the meaning of the non-occurrence of one thing due to the existence of another, and the meaning of tahdid (urging, reproach). Except that when it is intended in this sense, it is followed only by an explicit verb or an implied one. And when the first meaning is intended, it is followed only by an explicit noun or an implied one, according to the Basrans. What is meant here is the second, that is: "Why do you not bring us ﴿the angels﴾ who bear witness to the truth of your prophethood and support you in warning, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?﴾ Or they punish us for denying [you], as the disbelieving nations came upon their messengers ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾ in your claim. For God Almighty's power to do that is beyond doubt, and likewise your need for it in carrying out your mission, since we will not believe you without that. Or: if you are among that company of truthful messengers whose disbelieving peoples were punished for denying them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 8:**

﴿We do not send down the angels﴾ with the nun, in the active form, with God's pronoun as subject, from *tanzil* (sending down gradually). It is also read as *min al-inzal* (from *inzal*, sending down). It is also read as *tunazzalu* (*tunazzalu*, present tense, from *tanzil*) in the passive form, and as *tanazzalu* (from *tanzil* with one of the two taas elided), and as a past tense verb from it and from *tanzil*, and from the triliteral root. This is a statement directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), as a reply to them concerning their quoted saying, and a rejection of their false demand. Because the demand for a reply is so strong, its rejection was placed before what is a reply to the beginning of their speech, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ ... the verse. This is like what occurs in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Only God will bring it to you﴾, for although it is a reply to their saying: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾, it was placed before His saying: ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you﴾ ... the verse, while it is also a reply to the first of their words, which is their saying: ﴿O Noah, you have disputed with us﴾, because of what has been mentioned of the strength of its requirement for a reply, and so that one of the two replies would be connected to the question. In the reverse order, each of the two replies would be separated from its question. The deviation from applying the reply to the apparent meaning of their speech, which is in the context of a demand, would be to say: "You do not bring them with them," to indicate that they have erred in the expression just as they erred in the demand, and that the angels, because of their high rank, are too exalted to be attributed with mere coming, which includes movement from one of two equal places to the other, but rather [coming] from below to above, and that the destination of their movements be those unbelievers, and that they enter under the dominion of any of the human beings. What befits their station is descent from their lofty position, and that this be by way of sending down from the presence of the Lord, the Majestic, ﴿except with truth﴾, that is: accompanied by the aspect with which it is right for the sending down to be accompanied, of what wisdom requires and the divine practice follows, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾. What they demanded of sending down, for the purpose of testimony before them, while they are what they are, and their rank in lowliness and humiliation, is a rank that scarcely enters under soundness and wisdom at all, for that belongs to the category of sending down by revelation, which is scarcely opened except to the noble prophets and the perfect individuals among (p-68) the believers. How then [would it be] for such wretched unbelievers? What does fall under wisdom, in general, in their case is sending down for punishment and annihilation, as was done to their like among the earlier nations. Had that been done, they would have been utterly annihilated. ﴿And they would not then be given respite﴾: the answer of the condition is omitted, and in this there is an indication that their premises produce the opposite of what they sought, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾. The author of the *Nazm* (composition) said: the word *idhan* (then) is composed of *idh* (when), which is a noun meaning "time." You say: "I came to you when you came to me," that is, "at the time you came to me." Then *an* was added to it, and it became *idh an*. Then they found the hamza heavy and dropped it. So the occurrence of the word *an* is evidence of a verb being implied after it, and the estimate is: "And they would not be given respite, when what they requested had been [done]." The meaning is: had We sent them down, they would not have been delayed, like the practice of the rest of the denying and mocking nations. Despite their deserving that, the pen of decree has run with delaying their punishment until the Day of Resurrection, as has been summarized in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them﴾ ... etc. And the wisdom intervened between them and their annihilation, because knowledge and will are attached to increasing them in punishment, and to the faith of some of their offspring. As for arranging the faith of some of them within the thread of wisdom, the context of explaining their persistence in unbelief and corruption, and their obstinacy in arrogance and enmity, forbids it. This is what the inimitability of the Glorious Revelation requires. As for what has been said to explain why the sending down does not accord with wisdom, namely that they would then be believers out of compulsion, or that there is no wisdom in the angels coming to you in forms you can see, for that would only increase you in confusion, or that the sending down of the angels is only with truth, and the benefit being achieved by their descent, and God, exalted is He, knew from the state of these unbelievers that if He had sent the angels down to them, they would have remained persistent in their unbelief, so their descent would become futile and vain and not truth. With each of these failing, because the rest is cut off, it does not follow from supposing that any of these occurred that the punishment is hastened, which is what His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they would not then be given respite﴾ indicates. This is on the assumption that their demand for the angels' coming was for the purpose of testimony. Or on the assumption that it was for their punishment. The meaning then is: We do not send down the angels for punishment except with a sending down accompanied by truth, which wisdom requires and benefit necessarily demands, in such a way that there is no escaping it. Had We sent them down as they proposed, that sending down would not have been accompanied by what wisdom requires, which necessitates delaying their punishment until the Day of Resurrection, not out of kindness to them, but as an intensification against them, as has passed before. And since attributing their sending down for punishment to its not according with wisdom carried a kind of implication that they did not deserve punishment, the expression was turned away from what the apparent meaning requires to what the noble composition is upon. It is as if it were said: "Had We sent them down, they would not have been given respite, and that is not in accordance with the wisdom that requires delaying their punishment, so that their chastisement is intensified." It has also been said: the intended meaning of *al-haqq* (truth) is revelation. It has also been said: it is punishment. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾ This is a refutation of their denial of the revelation and of their mockery of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on account of it, and a consolation for him. That is: We, by the greatness of Our majesty and the exaltedness of Our dignity, have sent down that Reminder which they denied, and they denied its descent upon you, and by this they attributed madness to you. They also ignored its Sender, since they framed the verb in the passive, as an indication that it is a matter with no source and an act with no agent.

﴿And indeed, We are its guardian﴾ from everything that is unfitting for it, so that there enters into this: their denial of it and their mockery of it, entering it first and foremost. Thus it is a threat to the mockers. As for guarding it merely from distortion, addition, omission and the like, this does not befit the context. The preferred reading is therefore to take the guarding as being from everything that would impugn it, such as attacks upon it and disputing its truth. It is also permissible that its preservation be meant by its inimitability, as evidence that it is sent down from Allah, exalted is He, for if it were from other than Allah, addition, omission and contradiction would have found their way into it. In the construction of the two sentences there is a indication of the perfection of Majesty and Glory, and of the magnificence of the status of the revelation, which is not hidden. In presenting the second with a nominal sentence there is an indication of the permanence of the guarding. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best. It has been said: the pronoun in the genitive refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. And the placement of this statement, although it is an answer to the beginning of their false speech, serves as a rebuttal of it on account of what was mentioned just before, and because of its connection to what follows it in His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 10:

﴿And We certainly sent﴾ i.e., messengers. It is not mentioned because what follows it indicates it.

﴿before you﴾ is related to "sent," or to an omitted element which is an adjective (na't) of the omitted object, i.e., messengers who were before you.

﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ i.e., their groups and factions. It is the plural of shi'ah (sect), which is a group agreed upon a path and a creed, from shaa'ahu (he followed him) when one follows him. Its annexation to "the former peoples" is, according to al-Farra', an annexation of the qualified to its qualifier, and according to the Basrans, an annexation resulting from the omission of the qualified, i.e., the sects of the former nations. The meaning of sending them among them is making each of them a messenger among a group of them so that they would follow him in everything he brings and in what he leaves of the matters of religion.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 11:**

﴿وَما يَأْتِيهِمْ مِن رَسُولٍ﴾ The intended meaning is the negation of a messenger coming to each people (*shi'ah*, "group") specifically for his own group, not the negation of every messenger coming to each one of those groups all together, or in turn (*'ala sabil al-badal*, "alternately"). The form of the present tense (*al-istiqbal*) is used to bring the scene vividly before the mind, in the manner of narrating a past situation (*hikayat al-hal al-madiyah*, "narrating a past state"). For *ma* (negation) does not enter, in most cases, upon a present-tense verb except that it carries the sense of the present state, and does not enter upon a past-tense verb except that it is close to the present state. That is: no messenger, specific to one of those groups, came to a group from among those groups ﴿إلا كانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ ("except that they mocked him"), as these disbelievers do.

The clause (*al-jumlah*) is in a place of accusative (*mahall al-nasb*) as an anticipated circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddarah*) from the pronoun of the object in ﴿يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾, if the intended meaning of the coming (*al-ityan*) is its occurrence (*huduthuh*). Or it is in a place of nominative (*mahall al-raf'*), as a descriptive clause (*sifah*) of *rasul*, since its place is nominative by being the agent (*al-fa'iliyyah*), meaning: "except a messenger they used to mock." As for the genitive (*al-jarr*) reading as a descriptive clause, by consideration of its wording (*bi'tibar lafzih*), it would lead to the addition of *min* of comprehensiveness (*min al-istighraqiyyah*) in an affirmative context. It is permissible that it be accusative by way of description (*al-wasfiyyah*), by assuming the described noun to be accusative as an exception (*al-istithna'*), although the preferred reading is nominative by way of substitution (*al-badaliyyah*).

This, as you see, is a consolation (*tasliyah*) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that this is the custom of the ignorant with the prophets (ʿalayhim al-salam). And since the Messenger was accompanied by a Book from Allah the Exalted, their mockery of the Messenger included their mockery of the Book. For this reason it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 12:

﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ ("Thus") is a reference to what the preceding discourse indicates: the sending down of revelation accompanied by mockery. That is, "like that way of threading (al-salk) which We threaded into the hearts of those mockers of their messengers, and of what they brought of the scriptures." ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ ("We cause it to enter"), i.e., the Reminder (al-dhikr), ﴿فِي قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ ("into the hearts of the guilty"), i.e., the people of Makkah, or the category of the guilty in general. So they enter into it (the Reminder) in an initial manner of entry. Its place in the grammar is the accusative, being either an adjective (na't, a word modifying a noun) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar, the noun denoting the action), or a circumstantial accusative (hal, a word describing the state of the subject or object) of it. That is: "We cause it to enter an entry like that entry," or "We cause the entry to occur in a state of being like it," i.e., accompanied by mockery, not accepted in the way that wisdom requires, for they are among those forsaken, having no entitlement to accept the truth. The use of the present tense (sighat al-mudari') is either because the thing likened to it, which is the threading occurring among the earlier nations, is held to be existent, or to indicate the bringing of the image to mind. And al-salk (threading): inserting one thing into another. It is said: "I threaded the thread into the needle" (p-70) and "the spear into the one stabbed."

﴿They do not believe in it﴾, i.e., in the Reminder, is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the pronoun in نَسْلُكُهُ (*naslukuhu*), meaning: "not believing in it." Alternatively, it is an explanatory clause (*bayan*) for the preceding sentence, and so it has no grammatical position (*mahall*). The pronoun has been taken to refer to mockery, and in that case the explanatory reading is the only one that fits. However, the pronoun in the preposition phrase may also be taken to refer to mockery, with the بَاء (*ba'*) meaning "accompaniment": "We cause mockery to enter their hearts while they are not believers in its accompaniment." The circumstantial clause is either anticipated (*muqaddarah*) or simultaneous (*muqarinah*), to indicate that their disbelief accompanies the insertion, as in His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾. ﴿And the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾, i.e., their practice has already gone by, which God established in destroying them when they did what they did of denial and mockery. This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), brought as a supplement to consolation and as an explicit warning and threat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 14:

﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven﴾ — that is, upon these obstinate ones who made demands — ﴿a gate from the heaven﴾: that is, a gate of some sort, not one of its well-known gates, as it has been said: "And We made easy for them the ascent and the climbing up to it," ﴿and they remained in it﴾ — in that gate — ﴿ascending﴾ by means of an instrument or otherwise, seeing the wonders therein with their own eyes, as the continuance (ẓalla) indicates; or, [it means] the angels who were asked to come to them remained ascending in that gate, seeing it with their own eyes, becoming clear-sighted throughout the length of their day.

﴿لَقالُوا﴾ [they would surely say], out of their extreme obstinacy, their excessive stubbornness in denial, and their evasion of accepting the truth.

﴿إنَّما سُكِّرَتْ أبْصارُنا﴾ [Our eyes have only been dazzled]: that is, they were blocked from perception by intoxication (al-sukr). This is what the lightened reading (al-takhfif, in which the word is recited without doubling the letter, as سَكِرَتْ) indicates. Or they were bewildered, as supported by the reading of one who recited سَكِرَتْ, meaning: became bewildered.

﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾ [Nay, we are a people bewitched]: Muhammad (ﷺ) has bewitched us, as they said whenever the other manifest signs appeared. The two restrictive and corrective particles, إنما (only) and بل (nay), indicate that they assert this definitively, and that what they see has no reality, but is merely something imagined to them by sorcery. The nominal form of the second clause (جملة اسمية, a sentence beginning with a noun) indicates the continuity of its meaning. Placing it after the sealing of their eyes serves to explain their denial of anything other than what they see. The ascent of each of them into the sky, though it may be visible to others, is known to each person by his own direct perception, apart from sight. Yet they claim that this is another kind of sorcery, distinct from the blinding of the eyes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 16:

﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky constellations (buruj)﴾ — palaces (qusur) through which the planets (al-sayyarat) move. These are the well-known twelve constellations (al-buruj al-ithna 'ashara), differing in their forms and properties, as indicated by observation (al-rasd) and experiment (al-tajriba), together with what the majority of scholars agree upon regarding the simplicity (basatah) of the heavens. As for "al-ja'l" (placing/making): if it is taken in the sense of creating and originating (al-khalq wa'l-ibda'), which is the apparent meaning, then the preposition phrase is connected to it. If it is taken in the sense of making into something (al-tasyir), then it is a second object (maf'ul thani) connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "We made constellations existing in the sky."

﴿And We adorned it﴾ — that is, the sky — with those constellations of differing shapes, and with the stars, whether they are planets or fixed stars.

﴿for the beholders﴾ — those who look at it. The meaning of adornment is then apparent. Or [it means] for those who reflect, take heed, and draw inference from this upon the power of its Measurer and the wisdom of its Governor; so its adornment is its arrangement in a wondrous order that brings about good effects.
And We guarded it from every accursed Satan, (p-71) stoned with meteors, so that he cannot ascend to it, whisper to its inhabitants, act within it, or learn of its affairs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 18:

﴿Except him who steals a hearing﴾ Its position (i'rab, grammatical analysis) is the accusative, as an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil) if "guarding" (al-hifz) is interpreted as preventing the devils from approaching the heavens altogether and from gaining any knowledge of what is in them in general; or as an exception of the disconnected kind (istithna' munqati') if that is interpreted as preventing them from entering the heavens and from acting within them. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: they were not barred from the heavens; then when 'Isa (peace be upon him) was born, they were barred from three heavens, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, they were barred from all the heavens. Istiraq al-sam' (stealing a hearing) means snatching it secretly (ikhtilas, stealthy seizing). It is used as a figure for their brief snatching from the dwellers of the heavens, by the affinity that exists between them in substance, or by inference from the circumstances.

﴿So there follows him﴾ i.e., he pursues him and overtakes him, ﴿a flame (shihab)﴾, a burning blaze, namely a bright fire-brand; it may also be applied to the stars and to spear-points, because of the gleam in them, ﴿clear﴾, its matter being manifest to those who see. Ma'mar said: I said to Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri: "Were stars being hurled in the Jahiliyyah?" He said: "Yes." And the star falls and the devil is struck by it, so it kills him or leaves him deranged, lest he return to stealing a hearing; then it returns to its place. He said: "Have you considered the words of Him, Exalted: ﴿And we used to sit in it in positions for listening﴾ ... (the verse)?" He said: "It was made more severe, and its matter was intensified when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent." Ibn Qutaybah said: The stoning was before his (ﷺ) mission, but it was not under such intense guarding as after his (ﷺ) mission. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The devils mount one upon another up to the lowest heaven, stealing a hearing from the angels; so they are struck with the stars, and it never misses. Among them is one who is killed, and among them is one whose face, side and hand are burned wherever Allah the Exalted wills, and among them is one who is left deranged, so he becomes a ghoul and leads people astray in the deserts. Al-Qurtubi said: They differed as to whether the shihab kills or not. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it wounds, burns and deranges, but does not kill. Al-Hasan and a group said: it kills. He said: The first view is more sound.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 19:

﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾: "spread it out" (basatnaha). It is in the accusative (naṣb) by way of omission (ḥadhf) under the condition of tafsir (explanatory supplement). It was not read in the nominative (raf') because the accusative is preferred for coordination (ʿaṭf) upon the verbal clause (al-jumla al-fiʿliyya), I mean His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We have certainly placed...﴾ and so on. And so that it agrees with what follows it, I mean His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We cast into it firmly set mountains (rawasi)﴾, that is: mountains that are fixed firmly. Its explanation has already passed at the beginning of al-Ra'd.

﴿And We caused to grow in it﴾, that is: in the earth, or in it and in its mountains, ﴿of every thing weighed (mawzun)﴾ by the balance of wisdom, in its essence, its attributes, and its quantity. It has been said: that which is weighed of gold, silver and other things; or of every thing that is pleasing and suitable; or that which is weighed and measured of the doors of blessing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 20:

﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood﴾ That by which you live, of food and clothing and other things, whatever on which survival depends. It is written with a clear yā' (ya). It has also been read with a hamza, likening it to al-shamā'il (the hamza form, as in "shamā'il" being read as "sham'il").

﴿and [We have made provision] for those whom you do not provide for﴾ This is coordinated with ma'āyish (means of livelihood), or with the place of lakum (for you), as if it were said: "We have made for you means of livelihood, and We have made for you those whom you do not provide for, from among dependents, slaves, servants, animals, and the like," by way of taghlīb (giving precedence to the stronger term). Mentioning them under this description serves to refute the assumption that they are supported by you, and to establish that Allah the Exalted is the One who provides for them and for you. Or the meaning is: "We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and [We have made provision] for those for whom you are not providers."

(p-72) ﴿وَإنْ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ "In" is for negation, and "min" is extra, for emphasis. "Shay'" (thing) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'). That is: there is not any thing among the possible things, so that what has been mentioned enters into it at the first level of inclusion. ﴿إلا عِنْدَنا خَزائِنُهُ﴾ The adverbial phrase ("indana," with Us) is the predicate of the subject. "Khaza'inuhu" (its treasuries) is nominative, either as its agent (fa'il), since the phrase depends on it, or as its predicate (khabar) of it. The clause is the predicate of the first subject. "Khaza'in" is the plural of "khizana" (treasury, storehouse), which is only the place where precious wealth is kept. By custom it came to be applied to the treasuries of kings and sultans that hold the provisions of people. The things within His power, Exalted is He, which are not reached for enumeration and are included under His all-encompassing power, are likened to treasuries in that they are hidden from the knowledge of the worlds and protected from the reach of their hands, despite their complete need for them and their desire for them, and in that they are prepared and readily available for His bringing into existence and His forming. So whenever His will is related to their existence, they come into being without delay, like the precious wealth stored in royal treasuries. Thus the mention of "treasuries" is by way of imaginative metaphor (isti'ara takhyiliyya).

﴿وَما نُنَزِّلُهُ﴾ That is: We do not bring into existence, and We do not form any of those things in a state of being combined with any other thing.

﴿إلا بِقَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾ That is: except in a state of being bound to a specific measure which wisdom requires and which the will that follows it calls for, not by what power would require, for that is unlimited. The specification of each thing with a particular attribute, a particular measure, and a particular time, to the exclusion of anything else, while all are equal in possibility and in the suitability of power's relation to them, necessarily requires a wisdom that makes each thing specific to what it is specific to. This explanation is the secret of why things are not formed in the abundance that exists in the treasuries of power. This (phrase) is either a coordination (ʿatf) upon an implied element, meaning: "We send it down, and what We send down..." etc., or a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to what came before, meaning: "With Us are the treasuries of every thing, while the state is that We do not send it down except in a known measure." The first is to show the vastness of power; the second is to show the utmost wisdom. Since the bringing forth of this occurs by way of grace from the upper world to the lower world, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾, and since it occurs gradually, it is expressed by "tanzil" (sending down), and the present-tense form indicates continuity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 22:

﴿And We sent the winds﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "We made for you therein means of livelihood (maʿayish)," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ) to confirm what preceded and to reinforce what follows. That is: We sent the winds ﴿fertilizing﴾, i.e., ﴿carrying﴾ (ḥawāmil). The wind that brings good by producing rain-bearing clouds is likened to a pregnant woman carrying (al-ḥāmil), just as that which is not so is described as barren (ʿaqīm). Or [it means] ﴿fertilizing﴾ (mulaqqiḥāt) the trees and the clouds. Its counterpart is the word al-ṭawā'iḥ, in the sense of al-muṭīḥāt, in the line of verse:

؎ And one who is struck by what the calamities (al-ṭawā'iḥ) bring down

That is, the destroyers (al-muhlikāt). It has also been read as "wa-arsalna al-rīḥa" (singular), with the intent of the genus. ﴿So We caused water to descend from the sky﴾ after We had produced, by those winds, a rain-bearing cloud, ﴿water, and We gave it to you to drink﴾, that is: We made it for you as drink (suqyan), and this is more eloquent than "saqaynākumūhu," because of what it indicates of making water prepared for them, so that they benefit from it whenever they wish.

﴿And you are not its storers﴾ denies of them what He affirmed for His own majesty in His words: ﴿And there is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us﴾. It is as if it were said: We are the ones able to bring it into being, to store it in the clouds, and to send it down, and you are not able to do that. It has also been said: you are not its storers after We have sent it down into the pools, wells and springs; rather, We store it in them, so that We make them a drink for you, even though the nature of water requires that it sink into the ground.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 23:

﴿And indeed, it is We who give life﴾ by bringing life into some of the bodies that are receptive to it. (p-73) ﴿and cause death﴾ by removing it from them. The giving of life and causing of death may be generalized to include animals and plants. The placement of the pronoun (nahnu, "We") first serves to restrict (hasr), and it is either an emphatic affirmation of the first (pronoun), or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the verb, and the whole clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). It is not permissible for it to be a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, ḍamīr al-faṣl), not because the lam (of emphasis) prevents that as has been said, for the grammarians (al-nuhat) permitted the entry of the lam of emphasis upon the separating pronoun, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative (al-qasas al-haqq)﴾. Rather, it is because it did not occur between two nouns.

﴿And We are the inheritors﴾, meaning: the ones who remain after the passing away of all creation, the owners of dominion when the period of metaphorical dominion (al-mulk al-majazi) has ended, the ones who hold authority over all things, first and last. They have no disposal except the apparent (suri) disposal and metaphorical dominion. In this there is an indication that the later one is not an heir of the earlier one, as appears from the outward circumstances.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 24:**

﴿And We certainly know those among you who go before (in birth and death)﴾ — i.e., those among you who precede (others) in birth and death.

﴿And We certainly know those who come later﴾ — i.e., those who come after (others) in birth and death, or those who have not yet come out of the loins of their fathers, or those who have not yet been born; or those who precede in Islam and in jihad and hasten to obedience, and those who lag behind in that. Nothing of your conditions is hidden from Us. This is an explanation of the perfection of His knowledge after the argument for the perfection of His power, for whatever indicates it is evidence of it. And in the repetition of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly know﴾, there is what is not hidden of the indication of the utmost emphasis.

It is said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encouraged (people) to the first row, so they crowded upon it, and this was revealed. It is also said: "A beautiful woman used to pray behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so some people moved forward so as not to see her, and others held back so that they could see her, and this was revealed." The first (explanation) is the one that fits what precedes and what follows it of the saying of Allah, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 25:

﴿And indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them﴾, i.e., for the recompense. The placement of the pronoun of majesty (damir al-azamah, the emphatic pronoun of greatness) indicates that He is the One capable of gathering them, and the only One who undertakes it, because they used to deem that far-fetched and reject it, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ That is: it is He alone who will gather them. In the shift (iltifat, a shift in grammatical person) and the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) there is an indication of the cause of the ruling. In the attribution to his pronoun ﷺ there is an indication of kindness toward him, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise⦆ — possessing perfect wisdom and perfecting His actions, for wisdom is an expression for knowledge of the realities of things as they are, and performing actions as they ought to be. ﴿All-Knowing⦆ — whose knowledge encompasses everything. Perhaps the mention of the attribute of wisdom first is to announce that it necessitates the gathering and the recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 26:

﴿And We certainly created man﴾, i.e., this species, by creating its origin, and its first individual, in a wondrous creation, enfolding within it the creation of all its other individuals in a summary manner, as its verification has passed in Surat al-An'am.

﴿from clay of sounding dry sand﴾, from dry clay not baked, which makes a sound (yusalsilu), i.e., it produces a sound when struck. It has been said: if you imagine in its sound a prolongation, it is ṣalīl; and if you imagine in it a reverberation, it is ṣalṣala. It has also been said: it is an intensive form of ṣalla, when it has become foul.

﴿from black mud altered﴾, from clay that has changed and blackened through long exposure to water. It is an adjective of ṣalṣāl, i.e., from ṣalṣāl that came from ḥama'.

﴿molded﴾, i.e., shaped from the form of the face (sanat al-wajh), which is its image; or poured, from sanna al-ma', meaning he poured the water, i.e., cast in the form of a human, as images are cast from molten substances in molds. It has also been said: foul-smelling, in which case it is an adjective of ḥama'. According to the first two interpretations, its proper place would be as an adjective of ṣalṣāl, and it was placed after ḥama' only to alert that the beginning of its being molded was not in the state of its being ṣalṣāl, but in the state of its being ḥama'. As if He, glorified is He, poured out the black mud, and fashioned from it the image of a hollow human, which dried until, when struck, it sounded; then He changed it into another substance. So blessed is God, the Best of Creators.

﴿And the jinn﴾, the father of the jinn. It is also said that it refers to Iblis. It is permissible that it refers to the genus, as is apparent in the case of ﴿the human being﴾, since the diversification of the genus from one single created individual made of one single substance means that the entire genus was created from it.

It is also read with a hamza, as ﴿al-Jaann﴾ [the reading with hamza, al-Jaʾann]. Its accusative case (inṣāb) is governed by a verb that it explains (the verb "khalaqnāhu," "We created him," which is supplied and which it explains).

﴿We created him﴾, and this is stronger than the nominative (rafʿ), because it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the verbal sentence.

﴿before﴾, that is, before the creation of the human being. From this it becomes apparent that it is permissible for "those who came before" (al-mustaqdimīn) to refer to one of the two weighty ones (al-thaqalayn, i.e., jinn and humans), and "those who come after" (al-mustaʾkhirīn) to refer to the other, and that the address in His words ﴿from among you﴾ is to all of them.

﴿from the fire of the scorching wind﴾, that is, from the fire of intense heat that penetrates the pores. There is no impossibility in the creation of life from simple bodies, just as there is no impossibility in creating it from simple substances (al-jawāhir al-mujarrada), let alone from composite bodies whose majority of parts is the fiery part, for they are more receptive to it than those whose majority of parts is the earthy part. His words, Exalted is He, "from fire," are in terms of the predominant element, like His words, Exalted is He, "He created you from dust." The purpose of the noble verse, as it is, is to show the perfection of the power of God, Exalted is He, and to explain the beginning of the creation of the two weighty ones. Thus it serves as an alert to the second premise upon which the possibility of the resurrection (al-ḥashr) depends, namely the receptivity of the materials to gathering and to revivification.

﴿And when your Lord said﴾: it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (remember). Mentioning the time serves, as has been stated many times, to call to mind the events that took place in it. Mentioning the attribute of lordship (*rubbiyyah*), which indicates that a thing is brought gradually to the perfection appropriate to it, together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, indicates the reason for the ruling and honours him, peace and blessings be upon him. The meaning is: remember the time when He said, ﴿to the angels: "Indeed, I am going to create"﴾ in what follows. It also conveys, beyond the form of the present tense, that God is definitely the doer of this act, without any impediment that turns Him away from it or any hesitation that deflects Him from it.

﴿a human (*bashar*)﴾, that is, a person. It has been said that this is not the exact wording used at the time of address; rather, the apparent meaning is that they were told, "I am going to create a creature with such-and-such attributes," but in the reported speech only the name was retained. It has also been said: a dense body that can be touched and handled. And it has been said: a creature whose skin is exposed, without wool or hair.

﴿from dry clay (*salsal*)﴾: it is connected to *khaliq* (creator), or to an omitted word that serves as an attribute of its object, meaning: a human being made from dry clay that is ﴿from altered black mud (*hama masnun*)﴾, whose explanation has already been given. This does not conflict with what is said in God's words in Surah Sad: ﴿a human from clay (*tin*)﴾, because the absence, in the reported speech, of mention of the clay's attributes of change and blackening, and of the traces that befell it during formation, does not require that these be left unmentioned when the reported event actually occurred. The point is only that it was not mentioned there, being content with what was explained here.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 29:

﴿So when I have fashioned him﴾: that is, I shaped him in the human form and the human creation. Or: I fashioned the parts of his body by balancing his natural constitutions.

﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: the *nafkh* (breathing) is the passage of wind into the hollow of a body suitable to hold it and be filled by it. There is no actual blowing or anything blown here. Rather, it is an image (*tamthil*) for the bestowing, upon a receptive substance, of that by which life becomes actual. That is: when I have perfected its readiness and bestowed upon it the spirit by which it lives, which is of My command (p-75).

﴿Then fall down before him﴾: from *waqa'a yaqa'u* (to fall). This indicates that the command was not merely bowing, as some have said. That is: fall prostrate before him, ﴿prostrating﴾, as a greeting and a sign of honour. Or: prostrate to Allah, the Exalted, with him (peace and blessings be upon him) being in the position of the *qiblah* (the direction of prayer), since in him appeared the wonders of the traces of Allah's power and wisdom, as in the words of Hassan (may Allah be pleased with him):

"Was he not the first to pray toward your qiblah,
and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the Sunnah?"

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 30:**

﴿So the angels prostrated﴾, i.e., He created him, shaped him, then breathed into him the spirit, so the angels prostrated ﴿all of them﴾ (﴿كُلُّهُمْ﴾), such that none of them deviated, ﴿entirely﴾ (﴿أجْمَعُونَ﴾), such that none of them lagged behind another in that. There is no restriction of this meaning to the state (of prostration) alone; the emphasis also conveys it. The clear derivation indicates that the word carries the sense of gathering and togetherness, according to its lexical form. The principle in discourse is to interpret an expression according to the most complete state of the thing. There is no doubt that prostrating together is the most complete kind of prostration. However, this (word) has commonly come to be used as an emphasis and is placed in the position of each (individually) to convey the meaning of comprehensiveness, without regard to completeness. So when comprehensiveness is understood from another expression, it is necessary to observe the original sense, to preserve the speech from being rendered meaningless.

It has been said: it is emphasized with two emphatic words for the sake of intensifying the generality of this (meaning). As for whether their prostration here was consequent upon the conditional command mentioned (in this verse and in the one in Surah Sad), as this noble verse implies, or upon the immediate (unconditional) command, as what is found in other places requires? By the grace of God, Mighty and Majestic, we have been relieved of the burden of investigating it in the commentary on Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 31:

﴿Except Iblis﴾. This is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). It is so either because he was a single jinn, concealed among thousands of angels, and so he was counted among them by way of predominance (taghlib); or because among the angels there is a kind (jins) who reproduce, and he was of them. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾, it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) explaining the manner of the non-prostration that is understood from the exception, for the bare fact of not prostrating may occur with hesitation; and from this it is known that his non-prostration was accompanied by refusal (aba') and arrogance (istikbar). Alternatively, the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and what follows it is joined to it, meaning: "But Iblis refused to be with them." In this there is a demonstration of the utter feebleness of his opinion, in that three disobediences were combined into a single act of disobedience: opposing the command; arrogance together with contempt for Adam, upon him be peace; leaving the community (mufaraqat al-jama'ah); and refusing to be included in the company of those noble, honored ones brought near (to God).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 32:

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering the question: who said it, and what did Allah, exalted is He, say at that point? So it was said: He said, ﴿"O Iblis, what is wrong with you?"﴾, meaning: what reason? Not what purpose do you have. This is like what was said regarding His words, exalted is He: "What prevented you" ﴿from not being among those who prostrate﴾, i.e., from not being among those who prostrate ﴿to Adam﴾, although they, and their rank in honor, are of the same rank as them?! The rebuke at the time it occurred was not merely for his abstention from them, but for each of the three disobediences mentioned. Allah, exalted is He, said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿He said, "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?"﴾ and in Surat Sad: ﴿He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?"﴾. However, in the narration in each place only what is mentioned there was stated, relying on what was mentioned in another place, and to indicate that each one of those three disobediences is sufficient for the rebuke and for the manifestation of the invalidity of what he committed. The narration of the rebuke was altogether omitted in Surat al-Baqarah, Surat Bani Isra'il, Surat al-Kahf, and Surat Ta-Ha.

(p-76) ﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), i.e., Iblis. This is also a resumption (isti'nāf) built upon the question that the discourse leads to. ﴿Lam akun li-asjuda﴾ (I would not have prostrated): the lām (lam of emphasis) is for emphasizing the negation; i.e., it conflicts with my state and is not fitting for me, because I was created from the most noble of the elements, and the highest of them is that I should prostrate ﴿to a human being﴾ (basharin), i.e., a dense body, ﴿whom You created from clay, from black mud, molded﴾. Here he confined himself to a general allusion to his claim of superiority and the nobility of the substance, being content with what he expressed when he said: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾. The accursed one did not suffice with merely mentioning that he (peace be upon him) was made of dust, which is the lowest and most base of the elements, but rather went further to mention that he was created from it in its most base condition, namely as altered clay. In Sūrat al-A'rāf and Sūrat Ṣād he was content with what is related here, confining himself to recounting his mention of the creation of (peace be upon him) from clay; and likewise in Sūrat Banī Isrā'īl, where it is said: ﴿Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?!﴾ And in his answer there is evidence that Allah's words "What is the matter with you?!" are not an inquiry about the purpose but an inquiry about the cause. In his deviation from applying his answer to the question there is an attempt to evade the disputation; and how could he do so? It is as if he said: I did not refrain from obeying the command, nor from being counted among the ranks of the angels, but from what does not befit my station, namely submitting to one who is inferior. Allah abandon him: he proceeded along the lines of a barren analogy, and he slipped from the fact that what the sphere of virtue and perfection revolves around is adorning oneself with divine knowledge and being free of blameworthy dispositions, the most ugly of which are arrogance and defiance of the command of the Lord of the worlds, exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 34:

﴿He said, "Then get out of it﴾, i.e., from the host of the honored angels, not from the heaven. For his whispering to Adam, peace be upon him, in the Garden, occurred only after this expulsion. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So descend from it﴾ is not explicit on that point, for leaving from among the exalted assembly is a descent, and what a descent it is. Or [it means] from the Garden, on the basis that his whispering took place by way of calling out from its gate, as was narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri. Or [it means] by way of direct speech after he had contrived to enter it and approached him through the serpent, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. This does not conflict with his being expelled before all witnesses, given the profound wisdoms that this entails, ﴿for you are accursed﴾, expelled from every good and honor, for whoever is expelled is stoned with rocks, or [it means] a devil who is pelted with shooting stars. This is a threat that contains the answer to his doubt, for whoever opposes the text with analogy is accursed and rejected.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 35:

﴿And indeed, upon you is the curse﴾: the banishment from mercy. Since this comes from Allah, glorified is He, even though it is voiced upon the tongues of His servants, it was said in Surah Sad: ﴿And indeed, upon you is My curse﴾ ﴿until the Day of Religion﴾, that is, until the Day of Recompense and Punishment. This implies that His punishment and retribution for him are deferred until then, and that "the curse," despite its extreme dreadfulness, is not the recompense for his deed; rather, that is realized on that day. In this there is an awe-inspiring terror beyond description. As for making that the furthest term of the curse, it is not because the curse ends there; rather, it is because at that point he will be punished with such varieties of torment that the curse will be forgotten and will become as something that has passed away. It has also been said: the term was set at that point because it is the furthest limit that people ever set, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 36:

Since it is possible that the postponement of punishment, together with death, is like the case of all those disbelievers whose punishments were deferred to the Hereafter, the accursed one (al-La'in) sought to have his death postponed, as was related of him by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord, then respite me until the day they are resurrected."﴾

﴿He said: "My Lord, then respite me"﴾ meaning: grant me a reprieve and delay me, and do not cause me to die. The fa' (then) is connected to an implied element that the speech carries along with it, meaning: since You have made me one who is stoned (rajim), then grant me a reprieve ﴿until the day they are resurrected﴾, meaning: Adam and his descendants, for the reckoning after their annihilation. By this he intended to obtain a space to lead them astray, to take his revenge upon them, and to escape death, since it is impossible after the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 37:

﴿He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ The coming of the answer in the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), together with the indication that what he asked for extends to others, in a manner that signals the questioner was following them in this, is evidence that it is a report of the respite decreed for them from eternity (azalan), not a new granting (insha'). It was a particular respite that came in response to his supplication, meaning: "You are among the group whose terms were deferred from eternity, according to what the wisdom of creation requires." So the fa' (fa, "then") is not for linking the granting of respite itself to the request for it, but for linking the stated report to it, as in his saying:

؎ "So if You show mercy, then You are worthy of that"

For there is no possibility of making the fa' here link the eternal worthiness for mercy in Him, the Exalted, to the occurrence of a newly arising mercy. Rather, it links the report of that worthiness for mercy to its occurrence. His request for respite was a request for the postponement of death, since by it his being among them is realized, not a request for the postponement of punishment, as has been said. Placing him, in that, in the rank of those whose punishment is deferred until the Hereafter in the knowledge of God, the Exalted, from among the jinn who came before and those who come after from both groups (al-thaqalayn), does not suit the position of asking for respite while living. Also, that deferment is known from the attaching of the Day to the Religion (yawm al-din), along with its attaching in the question to the Resurrection (ba'th), as you have come to know.

In Surah al-A'raf he said: ﴿Give me respite until the Day they are raised﴾, he said: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾, with the time limit omitted and the address (nida') present, and the fa' in the request. The granting of respite is relying on what was mentioned here, and in Surah Sad. Indeed, the presentation of one statement in multiple styles is not rare in the Mighty Book. As for the claim that each style of the noble composition must have a situation that requires it, different from the situation of the others, and that what is related from the accursed one was uttered only once, and likewise his answer occurred only once, then if the situation of the dialogue requires one of the mentioned styles, it is the one that matches what the situation demands and reaches the level of inimitability; anything else falls short of the rank of eloquence, let alone rising to the markers of inimitability. Its verification has passed, by God's grace, in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿until the day of the appointed time﴾. This is the time of the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula), at which whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except those whom God, exalted is He, wills. It is also possible that the intended meaning of "the days" is one thing, and the difference in expressions is due to differences in perspectives. So the expression "the day of resurrection" (yawm al-ba'th) is used because the accursed one's aim in it is fulfilled; "the day of judgment" (yawm al-din) is used because of the recompense mentioned; and "the day of the appointed time" (yawm al-waqt al-ma'lum) is used for what has been mentioned, or because God, exalted is He, alone knows it. Thus it may be that the destruction of all creation, their resurrection and their recompense all occur on one day: the accursed one dies at its beginning, is resurrected in its middle, and is punished in the remainder of it.

It is related that between his death and his resurrection there are forty years of the years of this world, equal to the interval between the two blasts. It is also reported from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, may God have mercy on him, that he said: "I came to Medina wishing to see the Commander of the Faithful, Umar, may God be pleased with him. Then I came upon a great circle, and Ka'b al-Ahbar was in it, speaking to the people, and he was saying: 'When the time of death came to Adam, peace be upon him, he said: O Lord, my enemy Iblis will rejoice over me when he sees me dead, and he is granted respite until the day of resurrection?' He was answered: 'Yes, O Adam, you will indeed return to Paradise, and the accursed one will be delayed until the appointed respite, so that he may taste the pain of death together with the number of the first and the last.' Then He said to the angel of death: 'Describe to him how you will make him taste death.' When he described it, [Adam] said: 'O Lord, that is enough for me.' The people cried out and said: 'O Abu Ishaq, how is that?' He refused, but they insisted. So he said: 'God, glory be to Him, says to the angel of death, immediately after the first blast: I have placed in you the strength of the people of the seven heavens and the people of the seven earths, and I have clothed you today in all the garments of wrath and anger. Descend with My anger and My might upon My accursed one, Iblis, and make him taste death. Bear upon him in it the bitterness of the first and the last of the two weighty ones, multiplied manifold. Let there be with you seventy thousand of the Zabaniyah (guardians of hell), who are filled with rage and fury, and let each of them have a chain from the chains of Hell and a shackle from its shackles. Pull out his foul soul with seventy thousand of its hooks. Call Malik to open the gates of the fires.' Then the angel of death descends in a form such that if the people of the heavens and the earths looked upon it, they would die suddenly from its terror. He reaches Iblis and says: 'Stop for me, O wicked one, that I may make you taste death. How many lives have you reached, and how many generations have you led astray? This is the appointed time.' He said: 'The accursed one flees to the east, and there he finds the angel of death between his eyes. He flees to the west, and there he finds him between his eyes. He dives into the seas, and the seas seethe with him and do not receive him. He keeps fleeing in the earth, with no refuge and no shelter for him. Then he stands in the middle of the world, at the grave of Adam, and rolls in the dust from east to west and from west to east, until he reaches the place where Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down. The Zabaniyah have set up their hooks for him, and the earth has become like an ember. The Zabaniyah surround him and stab him with the hooks, and he remains in the agony of death-throes and punishment until God, exalted is He, wills.'" It is said to Adam and Eve: "Look today upon your enemy, how he tastes death." So they look and see what he is in of the intensity of the torment, and they say: "Our Lord, You have perfected Your favor upon us."

﴿قالَ رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ The *ba'* (بِ) is for swearing an oath (*li-l-qasam*), and *ma* is a verbal-source particle (*maṣdariyyah*), so the phrase means "by Your leading me astray." The answer (*jawab*) is ﴿لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهُمْ﴾, meaning: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make the acts of disobedience appear attractive to them," ﴿فِي الأرْضِ﴾, that is, "in the world, which is the abode of deception," as in His saying, ﴿أخْلَدَ إلى الأرْضِ﴾ ("he clung to the earth"). His swearing by the might of God, explained as His authority and dominance, does not contradict his swearing by this, for this is a branch of those (attributes) and an effect of them. So perhaps he swore by both together, and the (Qur'an) reports one oath at one time and the other at another time. Or the *ba'* is for causation (*lil-sababiyyah*), and his saying "*la-uzayyinanna*" is the answer to an omitted oath. The meaning is: "Because of your causing me to be led astray, I swear that I will do to them the same as what you did to me in causing them to be led astray: by making disobedience appear attractive and by adorning falsehoods." The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that stresses human free will and divine justice) interpreted "leading astray" (*al-ighwa'*) as relating to error (*al-ghayy*), or as causing it through God's command to him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him. They excused God's granting him respite and empowering him to lead the children of Adam astray by saying that God knew of him and of those who would follow him that they would die in disbelief and enter the Fire, whether they were given respite or not, and that granting him respite was an encouragement for whoever opposed him to earn greater reward. ﴿وَلأُغْوِيَنَّهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ means: "I will surely lead them all astray," that is, "I will surely bring them to error."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 40:

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them.﴾ Those whom You have made sincere (mukhlasin) for Your obedience, and whom You have purified from impurities (al-shawa'ib), (p-79) so that my scheming (kaydi) does not take effect upon them. And it is recited with a kasra on the lam (al-mukhlisin), meaning: those who have made their souls sincere (akhlasu) for God, exalted is He.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 41:

﴿He said, "This is a path"﴾ that is, a truth ﴿incumbent upon me﴾ that I must observe.

﴿Straight﴾ with no crookedness in it. The indication (al-ishara) is to what the exception (al-istithna') contains, namely the deliverance of the sincere ones (al-mukhlasin) from His (Iblis's) seduction. Or it is sincerity (al-ikhlas), in the sense that it is a path which leads to Me without crookedness or misguidance.
