The more apparent view is that this is because of what occurred in the words of Iblis when he said: ﴿Surely I will sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ ﴿Then I will surely come upon them from before them and from behind them﴾ ... the verse. It is also read as (ʿalayya) "upon Me," from the loftiness of honour (ʿulluw al-sharaf).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 42:

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾ — these are the ones referred to as "the sincere ones" (al-mukhlasin). ﴿You have no authority over them﴾ — no dominion or power to mislead. ﴿Except those who follow you among the misguided﴾. And in this, along with its being a confirmation of what the accursed one (al-La'in, i.e. Iblis) had said, there is an exaltation of the status of the sincere ones, a declaration of their rank, an indication that the claws of seduction are cut off from them, and that his misleading of the misguided is not by way of authority, but by way of their following him through their own bad choice.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 43:

﴿And indeed, Hell is their appointed place of promise﴾. That is: the appointed place of those who follow (al-Mutta'bi'un), or of those who go astray (al-Ghawun). The first is more fitting, and more effective in deterring one from following him. In it there is an indication that Hell is the place of the promise, and that what is promised is of a dreadfulness that cannot be described. ﴿All of them﴾ is either an emphasis (ta'kid) for the pronoun, or a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The governing element (al-'amil) in it is "the appointed place" (al-mawid), if it is taken as a verbal noun (masdar) with an elided genitive-governing noun (al-mudaf) understood, or the sense of the annexation (ma'na al-idafah) if it is taken as a noun of place (ism makan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 44:

﴿For it there are seven gates﴾ through which they will enter, because of their large number; or seven levels (tabaqat) which they will descend, according to their ranks in misguidance and following. And these are Jahannam, then Laza, then al-Hutama, then al-Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah.

﴿For every gate of them﴾ of the followers, or of the misguided, ﴿there is an allotted portion﴾: a specific group, set apart from others, according to what its preparedness requires. The highest of them is for the monotheists (al-muwahhidun). The second is for the Jews. The third is for the Christians. The fourth is for the Sabians. The fifth is for the Magians. The sixth is for the polytheists. The seventh is for the hypocrites. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that Jahannam is for those who claim divinity, Laza is for the worshippers of fire, al-Hutama is for the worshippers of idols, Saqar is for the Jews, al-Sa'ir is for the Christians, al-Jahim is for the Sabians, and al-Hawiyah is for the monotheists. Perhaps the restriction to seven is because the destructive things are confined to what is perceived through the five senses, and the requirements of the appetitive and irascible powers (al-quwwa al-shahawiyya wa al-ghadabiyya).

It has been read: with a damma on the zay, and with the hamza dropped and its vowel transferred to the letter before it, with shadda on it both in pause and in connection. ﴿Minhum﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying "juz'" (portion), or modifying its pronoun in the adverbial phrase (zarf), not "maqsum", because an adjective does not govern what precedes the noun it describes.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 45:**

﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾ are those who avoid following him (Satan) in disbelief and grave indecencies (fawahish), for other sins are expiated (by good deeds).

﴿in gardens and springs﴾ meaning: they will abide therein, remaining forever, and each one of them will have a garden and a spring from among these two, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. It was recited with the vowel kasra on the letter عَيْن (ʿayn) wherever it occurs in the Noble Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 46:

(p-80) ﴿Enter it﴾, with the implied sense of "say," as a command from God Most High to them to enter. It was also read as ﴿Cause them to enter it﴾ (adkhiluha), a command from Him, exalted is He, to the angels to bring them in. Al-Hasan read it as ﴿They were made to enter it﴾ (udkhilu), in the passive voice and the past tense form of the causative verb (al-idkhal). ﴿With peace﴾, meaning in a state of being joined with peace, that is, safe, or greeted with peace ("musallaman 'alaykum").

﴿Secure﴾, free from calamities and from cessation (of blessings).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 47:

﴿And We shall remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾. That is: resentment (ḥiqd) that existed in the worldly life. And it is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "I hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr will be among them, may the good pleasure of Allah be upon them all."

﴿As brothers﴾: a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) referring to the pronoun in His words, "in gardens" (fī jannāt), or to the subject of "enter it" (udkhulūhā), or to the pronoun in "secure" (āminīn), or to the pronoun that is the object of the idāfa (annexation), with the governing element being the meaning of the annexation. Likewise His words, ﴿on couches facing one another﴾. It is permissible that both of them be ṣifāt (descriptive adjectives) of "brothers," or ḥālān (circumstantial clauses) from its pronoun, since it carries the meaning of "facing one another" (mutaṣaffīn), and the second being a ḥāl from the concealed pronoun in the first. And it is related from Mujāhid: the couches turn with them wherever they turn, so they are facing one another in all their conditions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 48:

﴿Toil shall not touch them therein﴾, i.e., fatigue (nasab). This means that they shall have nothing in it that would necessitate the hardship of striving to obtain what is necessary for them, since everything they desire is attained without engaging in any labour at all. Or it means that such fatigue shall not befall them, even though they engage in vigorous movements, owing to the perfection of their strength. This clause is either a new, independent sentence (isti'naf), or a circumstantial clause (hal) following another circumstantial clause, or a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "muqabilin" (facing one another).

﴿Nor shall they ever be removed from it﴾, forever and ever, because the completion of the blessing lies in eternal abiding.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants﴾ — they are those whom He described as the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). ﴿That I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. This is a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded of promise and threat, and a confirmation of it. The mention of forgiveness here indicates that by "the God-fearing" is not meant those who guard against all sins, great and small; and the description of His Essence with these attributes, and with mercy, in the form of restriction (qasr) to the exclusion of punishment, is a notification (iidhan) that these two are among what His Essence necessarily entails, and that punishment only comes about through what necessitates it from outside.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants﴾ — they are those whom He described as the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). ﴿That I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. This is a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded of promise and threat, and a confirmation of it. The mention of forgiveness here indicates that by "the God-fearing" is not meant those who guard against all sins, great and small; and the description of His Essence with these attributes, and with mercy, in the form of restriction (qasr) to the exclusion of punishment, is a notification (iidhan) that these two are among what His Essence necessarily entails, and that punishment only comes about through what necessitates it from outside.

[And inform them] is a coordinate clause linked to "inform" (nabbi'), with "My servants" as its object. The purpose is to make them take heed of what happened to Abraham (upon him be peace) with his family: the good news amid fear, and of what befell the people of Lot of punishment, and the salvation of Lot (upon him be peace) with his family who followed him, amid fear; and to alert them to the descent of God's retribution upon the criminals, and to let them know that God's punishment is the painful torment.

[Concerning the guests of Abraham] Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him and his father) said: they were Gabriel (upon him be peace) and two angels with him. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: and seven with him. It was said: Gabriel, Michael and Israfil (upon them be peace). Al-Dahhak said: they were nine. From al-Suddi: they were eleven, in the forms of youths, their faces radiant. From Muqatil: they were twelve angels. The reason their mission title was not mentioned is that they were not sent to Abraham (upon him be peace), but to the people of Lot, as will be mentioned below.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 52:**

﴿When they entered upon him﴾ is in the accusative (naṣb, the grammatical case marking the object or adverbial), governed by an implied verb (fi'l muḍmar) that is coordinated with *nabbi'* ("inform"). That is, "and remember the time of their entering upon him." Or it is a predicate that has been omitted and is annexed to *ḍayf* ("guest"), meaning "the news of Abraham's guests when they entered upon him." Or it is governed by *ḍayf* itself, on the basis that it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar).

﴿Then they said﴾ at that point, ﴿"Peace"﴾ (*salāman*), meaning: we greet you with peace (*nusallimu salāman*), or "we have greeted," or "you are at peace (*salimta salāman*)."

﴿He said, "Indeed we are apprehensive of you."﴾ That is, "afraid" (khā'ifūn). Wajal (apprehension) is the unsettling of the soul in anticipation of something disliked. He, peace be upon him, said this when they refused to eat from the roasted calf (*al-'ijl al-ḥanīdh*, "the roasted calf") that he had brought near to them. This is because it was customary among them that when a guest arrived and did not eat their food, they assumed he had not come with good intentions, both at the beginning of their entering and afterwards. This is in keeping with God's words: ﴿But when he saw that their hands did not reach toward it, he disliked them and felt fear of them.﴾ Therefore there is no room for his fear, peace be upon him, to have been caused by their entering without permission or at an unsuitable time. For if that were the case, they would have answered then with what they answered then, and he, peace be upon him, would not have hastened to bring the food near to them. The reason it is not mentioned here is that it has been made clear elsewhere. Do you not see that his, peace be upon him, returning their greeting is not mentioned here either?

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 53:**

﴿They said, "Do not be afraid."﴾ *Lā takhaf*: do not fear. It is also read as *lā tāja̱l* and *lā tūjil*, from *awjalahu*, meaning he frightened him, i.e., "I will frighten him." And *lā tuwājil*, from *wājalahu*, with the same meaning as *awjalahu*.

﴿Indeed We give you good news﴾: this is a *isti'nāf* (a resumptive clause, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it), giving the reason for the prohibition of fear (*nahy 'an al-wajal*, the prohibition against apprehension). The one who is given good news hardly lets fear or sorrow approach his precinct. How could it be otherwise, when it is good news of his survival and the survival of his household in well-being and safety for a long time?

﴿of a boy﴾: he is Isaac, peace be upon him, as stated in the words of God Most High: ﴿So We gave them good news of Isaac﴾. Here he does not mention the good news of Jacob, peace be upon him, being content with what was mentioned in Surah Hud, that he would be "'Alim" when he reaches (maturity), and elsewhere ﴿a boy who is forbearing﴾.

"He said, 'Do you give me good tidings [of this] despite old age having touched me? Then of what do you give good tidings?'" Here the wonder of the Prophet (ﷺ)... 

Wait, I must translate faithfully; the passage refers to Abraham (عليه الصلاة والسلام), so I should render it as such, without adding notes.

**Translation:**

﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings [of this] even though old age has touched me?"﴾ His wonder at their good tidings of a son came in a state contrary to the birth-giving [normally expected]. He increased upon this, saying: ﴿"Then of what do you give good tidings?"﴾ That is: by what marvel do you give me good tidings? For good tidings of something whose occurrence is not ordinarily conceivable is good tidings without substance, or [he means]: by what means do you give me good tidings. It was also read with the nun being doubled and kasra-marked, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah).

﴿They said, "We give you good news of the truth."﴾ That is, of what will certainly happen, or of the certainty that has no doubt in it, or of a matter that is true. It is the command of God Most High and His word: ﴿So do not be one of the despairing.﴾ That is, do not be one of those who despair of this. God is able to create a human being without two parents, so how much more able is He to give a child to an aged old man and a barren old woman?

It was also read as (مِنَ القَنِطِينَ) (min al-qanitin, "of those who despair"). His intent, upon him be peace, was to magnify God's blessing within the framework of ordinary surprise, based on God's established way among His servants, and not to deem it improbable in relation to His power, glory be to Him. This is indicated by the words of the angels, ﴿So do not be of the despairing,﴾ rather than "of the doubters" or something similar. (p-82)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 56:

﴿He said: "And who despairs﴾? This is a rhetorical interrogative of denial, meaning: no one despairs ﴿of the mercy of his Lord except the misguided﴾, those who have strayed from the path of knowledge and right judgment, so they do not recognize the vastness of His mercy, the perfection of His knowledge and His power, just as Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said: "None despairs of the comfort of Allah except the disbelieving people." His purpose is to negate despair from himself in the most emphatic manner, i.e., "There is no despair in me regarding the mercy of the Exalted, and what I am saying is only to show that my state is incompatible with the overflowing of that great blessing upon me." The address to the attributes of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) and mercy contains an eloquence that is not hidden. It has also been read with a ḍamma and with a kasra on the nūn (yaqnaṭu and yaqinṭu), from qanaṭa (with fatḥa). This exchange was not with Ibrahim (peace be upon him) alone, among the angels; rather it was also with Sarah, as explained in Surah Hud. It is not mentioned here, being sufficed by what was mentioned there, just as that was not mentioned there, being sufficed by what was mentioned here.

**Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 57:**

﴿He said﴾, that is, Ibrahim, peace be upon him. His placing (of the clause) between his earlier statement and his statement ﴿"What is your business, O messengers?"﴾, that is, what is your matter and your weighty affair for which you were sent, apart from the good tidings? ﴿"O messengers"﴾ is explicit that between the two there is a suppressed (implied) speech, to which he alludes by this (clause) to its place, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿"He said: Shall I prostrate myself before one whom You created from clay?"﴾ ﴿"He said: Tell me, is this the one whom You have honoured above me?"﴾ ... the verse. For his last statement is not joined to his first statement, but is based upon the words of Allah the Exalted: "Then get out of it, for you are accursed" (15:34). The placing of ﴿"He said"﴾ between his two statements (indicates) the announcement that the second is not connected to the first and is not built upon it, but is other than it. Then his address to them, peace be upon them, with the title of messengership, after his earlier address had been free of that, together with its being prefaced by the particle "fa" (so), is evidence that their suppressed speech contained a statement that their coming was not merely for good tidings, but that they had another matter for which they were sent. So it is as if he, peace be upon him, said: "If your matter is not merely good tidings, then what is it?" There is no need to resort to the view that his knowledge, peace be upon him, that the whole purpose was not good tidings was due to their being a group of considerable number. Good tidings do not require a number, which is why one was sufficient in the case of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and Maryam. Nor is there need (to resort to the view) that they gave him the good tidings in the course of the situation to remove his fear, for if the good tidings had been the whole purpose, they would have begun with them. So reflect.

"They said, 'We have been sent to a people who are criminals.'" They are the people of Lut, but they are described with criminality, and they are referred to by way of indefinite expression (al-tankir) as a form of censure of them and as a way of showing contempt for them.

﴿Except the family of Lut﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from the pronoun in "criminals" (mujrimin). The meaning is: We were sent to a people who were all criminals, except the family of Lut. Thus the people and the sending include both the criminals and others, and the meaning is: We were sent to a people all of whom were criminals, except the family of Lut, so that We destroy the first (ones) and save the last (ones). What indicates this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾, meaning Lut and his family, ﴿all together﴾, meaning from what befalls the people. For it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) giving information of their deliverance because they were not criminals, or to clarify what was understood from the exception, namely the general non-inclusion of the punishment for them, since that may be the case by their condition being in-between. Or it gives the reason, for whoever is the object of deliverance is safe from the encompassing of the punishment. Or the exception is disconnected (munqati') from "people." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We will surely save them﴾, is connected to "the family of Lut" and functions in the position of the predicate of inna (khabar lakinna). On this basis, His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Except his wife﴾ is an exception (istithna') from "the family of Lut," or from their pronoun (damir). If it is taken as an exception from the pronoun alone, that is because the two rulings differ. The exception could also be from the family, unless ﴿Indeed We will surely save them﴾ is treated as a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). It is also read with the light (takhfif) pronunciation.

﴿We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾ means among those who stay with the disbelievers, so that she will be destroyed along with them. It is also read as "qadarna" with the light pronunciation. The verb of decreeing (taqdir) is construed with ﴿inna﴾ although this kind of construction is normally reserved for verbs of the heart, because the verb includes the meaning of knowing. It is also permissible to understand it as the meaning of "qalna" (We said), since decreeing (qada') is a kind of speech. Its origin is making one thing equal to the measure of another. The attribution of this decreeing to themselves (the angels), though it is the act of God, the Exalted, is due to their nearness to Him and their special standing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 61:

﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ This marks the beginning of an explanation of the manner in which the criminals were destroyed and the family of Lot was delivered, as was summarized in the exception (istithna'), and then the reason was explained in some detail. The apparent noun (al-muzhar) is placed in the position of the pronoun (al-mudmar) to indicate (li-l-i'dhan) that their coming was for the purpose of realizing what they had been sent with, namely the destruction and the deliverance. What is meant is not the very beginning of their coming, but their mere presence (muțlaq kaynunatihim) among the family of Lot, since what is related from him, peace be upon him, in the words of the Most High:

He said, "Indeed, you are an unfamiliar people." He (upon him be prayers and peace) said this only after the various means had run out and the excuses had failed him, when he had not witnessed from the messengers, in the face of his trials and the plots he endured from his people, who intended harm to them, the usual kind of help and support in what they undertook and abandoned, while he exerted himself to rescue them. It was an expression of disapproval at their abandonment of him and their failure to support him in such a distress that befell him because of them, since they were not directly with him in the means of defence and protection. This led him to say, ﴿If only I had against you some power, or could take refuge in a strong support﴾, as explained in detail in Surah Hud. He did not say it at the beginning of their arrival, out of fear that they would visit him with evil, as some have said. How could that be, when their reply, related by the words of the Exalted, is:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 63:

﴿They said: "Nay, we have brought you that about which they used to doubt.﴾ That is, the punishment with which you used to threaten them, so they doubted it and denied you. They had already peeled the staff (qasharu al-'asa), and had made the matter clear to him, upon him be prayer and peace. How then could distress and tightness of breast befall him after that? The word "bal" (nay/rather) is not a rejection of the fear mentioned above, in the sense of "we have not brought you that for which you deny us, but rather that which gladdens you and cools your eye." Rather, it is a rejection (idrab) of what upon him be prayer and peace had understood from the abandonment of his support. The meaning: "We did not forsake you, nor did we leave you between them and yourself; rather, we have brought you that which will destroy them, of the punishment about which they used to deny you when you threatened them with it." Perhaps the presentation of this dialogue before what took place between him and the people of the city of disputation was to hasten the mention of the good news of Lot, upon him be prayer and peace, of the destruction of his people and the deliverance of his family, following the mention of the good news to Abraham, upon him be prayer and peace, concerning both. Since it called for an explanation of how deliverance occurs and the arrangement of its beginnings, this was alluded to briefly; then he mentioned what the people did and what was done to them. He did not mind the change in the chronological order, trusting in its observance in other places. The attribution of bringing the punishment to him, upon him be prayer and peace, although it descends upon the people, is by way of entrusting the matter to him, not by way of its descending upon him, as if they had come to him and entrusted their matter to him so that he might send it upon them according to what he had been threatening them with.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 64:

﴿And We have brought you the truth﴾ That is: with the certainty in which there is no room for doubt or uncertainty, and that is their punishment. He expressed it thus (bi-dhalika) as an explicit affirmation of the negation of doubt concerning it. Or the intended meaning of "the truth" (al-haqq) is the report of the coming of the aforementioned punishment. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ is an emphasis on it, that is: We have brought you, in what We said, the true report (al-khabar al-haqq), that is, the one that corresponds to reality (al-waqi'). ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in that report, or in every statement, so that it serves as evidence of their truthfulness in it. According to the first reading, it is emphasis upon emphasis. His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 65:

﴿So travel by night with your family﴾ This begins the arrangement of the principles of deliverance, meaning: take them away during the night. It is also read as ﴿wasl﴾ (a joined reading, in which the initial hamzah is connected to the preceding word). Both readings come from ﴿al-isra'﴾ (night travel), which is travel during the night. It is also read as ﴿fa-sir﴾ (travel) from ﴿al-sayr﴾ (going).

﴿at some part of the night﴾ meaning during a portion of it, or during its latter part. The poet said:

Open the door and look at the stars: how much of the dark night is still upon us?

It was also said: it is after some good portion of it has passed.

﴿and follow behind them﴾ meaning be behind them, driving them on, hastening them along, and keeping watch over their condition. The choice of ﴿following﴾ over ﴿driving﴾, although driving is the actual intent of the command, may be for emphasis in this matter, since driving may involve going ahead of some while lagging behind others, and it usually entails neglecting the state of the one who lags. This is also tied to the prohibition on looking back, stated in the words of God Most High: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, that is, none of you, neither you nor them, ﴿look back﴾, lest he see the terror behind him and be unable to bear it, or lest what befell them befall him; or, let none of you turn away or lag behind for some purpose, lest the punishment strike him. It was also said that they were forbidden this so that they would prepare themselves for emigration; or it is a prohibition against tying the heart to what they left behind; or it is for the sake of hastening the journey, for one who looks back rarely avoids pausing even briefly. The absence of mention of an exception for the wife from the night journey, and the fact that looking back does not require its non-occurrence, is because, as you have learned repeatedly, what has been mentioned is sufficient in other places. ﴿And proceed to where you are commanded﴾ meaning to where God Most High has commanded you to go, which is Syria or Egypt. Omitting the two relative complements is according to the well-known broad usage (ittisa'), and choosing ''proceeding to'' what was mentioned over ''arriving at it'' and ''joining it'' is to signal the importance of deliverance and to observe the appropriateness between it and what preceded regarding the ones who remained behind.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 66:

﴿And We decreed﴾ i.e., We revealed to him (ﷺ) as something decreed; for this reason it was construed with "ila" (to). ﴿that matter﴾ is vague and is explained by ﴿that the root of these would be cut off﴾, which is in apposition (badal) to it. The use of the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) rather than a pronoun serves to indicate that they are characterized by their ugly attributes, on which the establishing of the ruling depends, i.e., "the root of these criminals." Using the passive form in place of the present tense is because it is more emphatic in indicating that the event has occurred. Also, [there is the matter of] the word "qada'" (decree), the expression of the punishment as "amr" (matter), the pointing to it with "dhalika" (that), its placement after the prepositional phrase, and its being vague first and then explained second, all of which indicate the grandeur and horror of the matter, which is not hidden. It was also read with a kasra (i.e., "inna"), as a resumption (istinaf, a new independent sentence), and the meaning is: they will be uprooted to the last of them, so that none of them remains. ﴿at dawn﴾ means entering into the morning, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to ﴿these﴾ or to the pronoun, and to "maqtu'" (cut off). Its plural form is for the sake of agreement with the meaning, since "dabir" (root/last remnant) here means "mudbirun" (those who turn their backs/depart), i.e., the last of these.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 67:

﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ This begins the narration of what the people did and said when they stood at the place of the guests, both in action and speech, and of what followed from it, after this had been alluded to in summary, as indicated. That is: the people of Sodom came to the dwelling of Lot, upon him be peace, ﴿rejoicing﴾, i.e., rejoicing at his guests, upon him be peace, in hope of them.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 15, verse 68:

﴿He said: "These are my guests."﴾ The word ḍayf (guest), in origin, is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is applied to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. Its application to the angels is according to his belief, peace be upon him, because they were in the appearance of guests. The emphasis (al-ta'kid) is not due to his denying them, but rather to affirm their being characterized by it, to show his care for their matter, his readiness to observe their rights, and his protecting them from harm. For this reason he said: ﴿So do not disgrace me﴾, that is: in their presence, by subjecting them to harm, so that they would know that I have no standing or sanctity with you; or, do not disgrace me by disgracing my guest, for whoever mistreats his guest has mistreated him. It is said: faḍaḥahu faḍḥan wa faḍīḥatan (he disgraced him), when he revealed of his affair what brings him shame.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 69:

﴿Fear Allah﴾ in your engaging in what would grieve me, ﴿and do not disgrace me﴾, i.e., do not humiliate me or dishonor me by assaulting those whom I have granted protection, with that vile deed. Since their assault upon them, after he (peace and blessings be upon him) had forbidden them from it by his saying, ﴿do not shame me﴾, had a greater effect upon him (peace and blessings be upon him) and brought more disgrace upon him, for an assault upon a neighbor before the protector becomes aware of it may be overlooked, whereas after he has become aware of it, and has taken a stand to protect and defend him, that is the greatest disgrace. He (peace and blessings be upon him) expressed what befalls him from their side, after the aforementioned prohibition, because of their obstinacy and their openly defying him, as a matter of disgrace, and he commanded them to fear Allah Most High in this matter. He did not explicitly forbid the very act of that abomination, because he knew that this would not benefit them. It has been said: the intended meaning is to fear Allah Most High in committing the abomination. However, this is not supported by his placing it between two prohibitions concerning two matters that relate to himself (peace and blessings be upon him). Likewise is the saying of the Exalted:

﴿Did we not forbid you from [receiving] all people?﴾ That is: from interfering with them by keeping them away from us, and from hosting them. The hamza (the interrogative particle) expresses denial, and the waw (the conjunction) is coordinating with an implied clause, meaning: Did we not warn you in advance and forbid you from that? For they used to attack every stranger with evil, and he, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), would forbid them from this to the best of his ability. They had also forbidden him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), from granting protection to anyone. So it is as if they said: What you mention of disgrace and humiliation came to you from your own side, not from ours, for had it not been for your interfering with what we ourselves confront, that state would not have overtaken you, and when he saw that they would not desist from what they were upon (p-86).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 71:

﴿He said, "These are my daughters"﴾ meaning the women of the people. For the prophet of every community stands in the position of their father, or they are literally his daughters; that is, "marry them." Previously they had been seeking them, but he did not grant them [access to them] because of their wickedness and their unsuitability, not because marriage between Muslim women and disbelievers was not legislated. In Surah Hud this was elaborated: ﴿If you are going to act [at all]﴾ meaning, to fulfil your desire, or [to do] what I tell you.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 72:**

﴿By your life﴾ is an oath by Allah, exalted is He, by the life of the Prophet (ﷺ), or an oath by the angels by the life of Lut, peace be upon him. The implied phrase is: "By your life, my oath." It is a dialectal form of the word for life, *'umr* (عُمُر), in which the oath is specifically used, out of preference for lightness, because it frequently occurs on people's tongues.

﴿Indeed they are in their intoxication﴾: their misguidance, or the intensity of their lust (*ghulma*), which removed their intellects and their ability to distinguish between error and correctness.

﴿Wandering blindly﴾: they are bewildered and persist in excess. How, then, would they hear advice? It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, and the clause is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraḍ*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 73:

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾ That is, the great, terrifying Cry. It was also said: it was the cry of Jibril (peace be upon him). ﴿at sunrise﴾ meaning they entered the time of the sun's rising.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 74:

﴿So We made its highest part its lowest⁠—﴾ "its highest" meaning the highest part of the city, or the highest part of their villages, and it is the first object of "We made" (ja'alna). His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿its lowest⁠﴾ is the second object of it, and it is more emphatic in terror and horror than the reverse, as has passed. ﴿And We rained upon them﴾ within the course of that, before the completion of the overturning, ﴿stones﴾ existing ﴿of sijjil⁠﴾, that is, of clay turned to stone, or of clay upon which was a writing. This has been explained in Surat Hud.

Verse 75: ﴿Surely in that﴾ — i.e., in what has been mentioned of the story — ﴿are signs﴾ — indications by which the reality of the truth may be inferred — ﴿for those who discern﴾ — i.e., those who reflect and exercise insight (mutafarrisin), who look steadily so that they come to know the reality of a thing through its mark.

Translation:

﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, the city, or the towns, ﴿is on a road that remains﴾, that is, a established path that people travel and see its traces.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, in that⁠﴾ — that is, in what has been mentioned of the city (al-Madinah), or the towns, or in their being on a route, i.e., people see them as they travel to and fro.

﴿is surely a sign⁠﴾ — a great one — ﴿for the believers⁠﴾ in Allah and His Messenger, for it is they who know that the punishment which befell them, which left their abodes as desolate ruins, befell them only because of their evil deeds. As for others, they attribute that to coincidence or to the positions of the celestial bodies. The use of the singular ﴿sign⁠﴾ after the plural used earlier is because what is witnessed here is the remaining traces, not the whole story, as in what came before.

(p-87) ﴿وَإنْ كانَ﴾ "In" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna," and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), which is its subject, is omitted; the lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqah). That is: "Indeed the matter was that ﴿the companions of the Thicket﴾ — and they are the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him — ﴿were truly wrongdoers﴾." The Aykah (the Thicket) is a tree that is intertwined and dense; most of their trees were the muql (a type of thorny tree), and they used to dwell in it. So God, exalted is He, sent him (Shu'ayb) to them ﴿wrongdoers﴾, going beyond the limit.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ with the punishment. It is narrated that God subjected them to the heat for seven days. Then He sent a cloud, and they took refuge beneath it, seeking coolness. God then sent forth from it a fire that burned them. This is the punishment of the Day of the Canopy (Yawm al-Zullah).

﴿And indeed they﴾ means Sodom and al-Aykah. It was also said that they are al-Aykah and Madyan, since he (peace be upon him) was sent to both of them, so the mention of one serves as a reminder of the other. ﴿were indeed on a clear highway﴾ means on a clear path. The imam (that which is followed, a model or guide) is the name for whatever one takes as a guide, and the path is called by this name. It is also used for the foundation of a building, and for the tablet on which something is written, because each of these is something that is followed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 80:

﴿And indeed the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers.﴾ He means Thamud, ﴿the messengers﴾, i.e., Salih. For whoever denies one of the prophets, peace be upon them, has denied them all, because they agree on monotheism and on the fundamentals that do not differ according to nations and eras. It has also been said that what is meant is Salih and those believers who were with him, just as it has been said: "al-Khubaybun," referring to Khubayb ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and his companions. Al-Hijr (the valley between Madinah and Syria) is a valley between al-Madinah and al-Sham, where they used to dwell.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 81:

﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾. These are the verses sent down to their Prophet, or the miracles of the she-camel: her drinking, her water, and her milk; or the proofs set up for them.

﴿But they turned away from them﴾, a total turning away; rather, they were opposing them, in that they did to the she-camel what they did.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 82:

﴿And they used to carve out houses from the mountains, feeling secure﴾ from collapse, from thieves breaking in, and from enemies destroying them, owing to their sturdiness; or from the punishment, because they reckoned that these would protect them from it. It is narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "We passed by al-Hijr with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged his mount on, and it hurried until he had left it behind."

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 83:

﴿So the Shout seized them at daybreak﴾. And thus it occurred in Surah Hud. It was said: Jibril (peace be upon him) shouted at them. And it was said: there came upon them from the sky a shout containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything on the earth, so their hearts burst within their breasts. And in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿So the Quake seized them﴾, i.e., the earthquake (al-zalzalah). Perhaps it is among the accompaniments of the Shout, which entail a violent agitation of the air that leads to it, as has passed in Surah Hud.

(p-88) ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾, i.e., it did not repel from them what had descended upon them, namely [the earnings] from building sturdy houses, abundant wealth, and numerous equipment. There is in this a mockery of them. The fa' (fa, "so") indicates the sequence of the non-availing that is specific to the time the punishment descended, as they had hoped, not the absolute non-availing, for that is a continuous matter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 85:

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth.﴾ That is: except as a creation bound up with truth, wisdom and benefit, in such a way that it does not suit the continuation of corruption and the establishment of evils. For this reason wisdom has required the destruction of the likes of these people, to repel their corruption and to guide those who remain toward righteousness. Or: except by means of justice and equity on the Day of Recompense for deeds, as is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Hour is surely coming﴾, so that Allah, Exalted is He, will take vengeance for you therein upon those who denied you. ﴿So forgive﴾, that is: turn away from them ﴿with a gracious forgiveness﴾, a gracious turning away, bear their harm, do not hasten to take revenge upon them, and deal with them in the manner of one who is forgiving and forbearing. It was said: this verse has been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Indeed, your Lord ﴿is the One who brings you to the utmost perfection﴾ [note: text reads "الَّذِي يُبَلِّغُكَ إلى غايَةِ الكَمالِ"]...

Let me correct and give the translation cleanly:

Indeed, your Lord, Who brings you to the utmost perfection, ﴿He is the Creator (al-Khallaq)﴾ of you and of them and of all existing things absolutely, ﴿the All-Knowing (al-'Alim)﴾ of your circumstances and their circumstances, in their details, so nothing of what passed between you and them is hidden from Him. Therefore He is worthy that you entrust all affairs to Him, so that He may judge between you. Or, it means: He is the One who created you and knew the details of your circumstances, and He knew that forgiving (al-safh) today is more righteous than the sword being more righteous later. So this is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to forgive under both interpretations. In the codex of 'Uthman and in that of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, it reads: "He is the Creator (al-Khaliq)," and al-Khaliq is suitable for both little and much, whereas al-Khallaq is specific to much.

﴿And We have certainly given you seven [of] the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an.﴾

"Seven": seven verses, which is the Fatihah. This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with them, and of al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on them. It has also been said that it means seven surahs, namely the long surahs (al-tiwal), the seventh of which is al-Anfal, and al-Tawbah, because the two are treated as one surah, and for this reason they are not separated by the basmalah. It has been said that it refers to Yunus, or to the seven Hawamim (the surahs beginning with Ha-Mim). It has also been said that it refers to the seven sahifas (sheets), which are the asbaʿ (the sevens).

﴿of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾: an explanation of "seven" by means of "tathniyah" (repetition), which is repetition. If the intended meaning is the Fatihah, which is the apparent meaning, then it is called "mathani" (oft-repeated) because its recitation is repeated in the prayer. As for its being repeated outside the prayer, as has been said, this is not of a kind that could be the basis for the name. Also, it is "repeated" by what is recited after it in the prayer. As for the repetition of its revelation, this is not a valid reason for the name, because it was already called by this name before its second revelation, since the surah is Meccan by consensus. If the intended meaning is other surahs, then the reason it is among the mathani is that each of these is repeated in recitation and in its wording, or in its narratives and admonitions, or that it is from "thana'" (praise), because it contains what is praise of Allah. Its singular is "mathnah" or "mathniyyah," an adjective of "ayah." As for the sahifas, which are the asbaʿ: this is because of the repetition of narratives, admonitions, promise, and warning, and other things that occur in them, and because of the praise of Allah Most High contained in them, as if they praise Him, glorified be He, for His acts and His beautiful attributes. It is also permissible that "mathani" refers to the Qur'an, for the reason mentioned first, since it is praised for its inimitability, or to all the books of Allah Most High, in which case "min" is partitive, and on the first view it is explanatory.

﴿and the Great Qur'an﴾: if "seven" is intended as verses or surahs, then it is the mention of the whole after a part, or the general after the specific. If it is intended as the asbaʿ, or the whole Qur'an, then it is the conjunction of one of the two descriptions with the other, as in his saying:

"To the lordly king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalions in the crush of battle."

That is: We have certainly given you what is called the seven oft-repeated, and the Great Qur'an.

﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾: do not raise your gaze with the aspiration of one who desires, and do not prolong your look ﴿toward what We have given enjoyment to﴾ of the adornments of this world, its ornaments, its beauties, and its splendor, ﴿as pairs, some of them﴾, meaning kinds of disbelievers. The various kinds of wealth and treasures in this world, compared with what you have been given, are utterly insignificant and not worth any regard at all. In the hadith of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given something better than what he has been given has belittled something great and magnified something small." It is related that seven caravans arrived from Busra and Adhri'at for the Jews of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, carrying kinds of bazz (fine cloth), perfume, jewels, and various other goods. The Muslims said: "If these goods were ours, we would strengthen ourselves with them and spend them in the way of Allah." It was said to them: "You have been given seven verses, and they are better than these seven caravans."

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, that they do not believe and do not join your followers in one row so that the weak among the Muslims might be strengthened by them. It was also said: the meaning is that they are the ones who enjoy it, and this is rejected by the word ʿalā (on/over), since their enjoyment of it cannot be a ground for grief over them.

﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾: that is, be humble toward them, be gentle with them, soften your side toward them, and be content of heart regarding the faith of the rich.
And say, "Indeed I am the clear warner" (al-nadhir al-mubin): that is, the one who warns, who makes manifest the descent of God's punishment and its arrival.

﴿As We sent down upon those who divided [the Scripture]﴾. It has been said that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And We have certainly given you seven of the often-repeated and the great Qur'an"﴾ ... etc. That is: We sent it down to you just as We sent down [the Scripture] to the People of the Book.

[p-90] Those who have made the Qur'an into fragments (*'idin*). That is: they divided it into true and false, when they said, out of obstinacy and hostility, "Part of it is true and agrees with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false and contradicts them." Or they divided it among themselves in mockery, as some of them would say, "Surat Al 'Imran is mine," and so on. Or they divided what they read from their books and distorted it, so that they affirmed some of it and denied some of it. The placement of His words, "﴿You shall surely strain your eyes﴾," has been taken as referring to the extension of what is meant by the discourse, namely consolation. This is followed by the remark that the context is too exalted for comparison, and that he, peace be upon him, was given what no one before or after him was given like. It has also been said that [the phrase] is connected to His words, "﴿Indeed, I am the clear warner﴾," for it carries the force of a command to warn. As if it were said: "Warn Quraysh with the like of what We sent down upon the dividers (*al-muqtasimin*), meaning the Jews, which befell the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, such that what is anticipated is treated as what has occurred." It has indeed occurred in this way. You should know that the punishment by which the threatened punishment is likened must necessarily be certain to occur and known to those who are warned, for only then is the benefit of the comparison realized, which is the affirmation and intensification of the warning. The punishment of the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, although it had not occurred at that time and had not been preceded by any promise or threat, was for them in a protected heedlessness and a disquieting doubt. Treating the anticipated as if it had occurred has a sublime place within inimitability, but only when it coincides with a context that calls for it, as in His words, "﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾," and its like. Moreover, restricting the dividing to the Jews merely because the punishment mentioned is specific to them, despite the Christians sharing with them in the dividing that results from agreement and disagreement, and in the dividing understood as distortion that encompasses both Scriptures, is restriction without a restricting cause. Indeed, restricting the punishment mentioned to them, although it is one of the results of the dividing, is restriction without a restricting cause. The relative pronoun has been made the first object of "warn," meaning: warn the fragmenters (*al-mu'addin*), who divided the Qur'an into sorcery, poetry, and fables, "﴿like what We sent down upon the dividers﴾." These are the twelve who divided the entrances of Mecca during the season, each sitting at one entrance to deter people from believing in the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. One of them would say, "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from among us, for he is a sorcerer," another would say, "He is a poet," and another, "He is a liar." God destroyed them on the day of Badr, and before that with afflictions. In this there is, along with what has been said before about the punishment to which the threatened punishment is likened not being an occurred event, nor known to those warned, nor one whose occurrence was promised, that there is no reason to restrict the attribute of fragmenting to them and to exclude the dividers from among them, although they are a model for them in this, since their describing the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, with what they described him, of sorcery, poetry, and lying, is a consequence of their describing the Qur'an in that way. And this is nothing other than the fragmenting itself. Nor is there reason to exclude them from the ruling of warning, given that the punishment that befell them was not of such severity that the punishment of others could be likened to it, nor was it specific to them, but general to both groups and others. Furthermore, some of those warned, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, perished before the destruction of most of the dividers on the day of Badr. Nor is there reason to place the second object before the first, as you see. It has also been said that it is an attribute of the object of "warner," put in its place, and that the dividers are those who sat at the entrances of Mecca, as has been explained. Along with what has passed, His words, "﴿as We sent down﴾," are explicit that this is the speech of God Most High and not the speech of the Messenger, peace be upon him. The excuse that this belongs to the category of what some close companions of a king say, "We have been commanded to do such-and-such," even though the command is the king's, as previously in His words, "﴿We have decreed that she is among those who remain behind﴾," is an evident artifice. Moreover, making the attributive adjective operate on the noun it qualifies is something the Basrans (*al-Basriyyun*, the grammarians of Basra) did not permit, so one must flee to the path of the Kufans (*al-Kufiyyun*, the grammarians of Kufa), or resort to making it a non-explicit object, meaning: "I am the clear warner with a punishment like the punishment of the dividers." It has been said that what is meant by the dividers is the group who swore together to attack Salih, peace be upon him, and God destroyed them. You know that their punishment, since it was established and known to those warned, as the Mighty Qur'an declares, is suitable to be the thing likened to the threatened punishment. But since the relative clause that follows it cannot be an attribute of the dividers, then whether we make it the first object of "warner" or make it the object of what the one warned implies, there is no benefit in mentioning the heading of fragmenting in the clause's scope, nor the heading of dividing in the sense mentioned in the scope of the second object. This is because such mention serves only to indicate the causal link of the clause or attribute to the ruling established for the relative pronoun and the described noun. Then there is no point of resemblance on which the likening of their punishment to the punishment of those others would turn, since they do not share the cause. The fragmenters are far from the dividing that is about affirming (*al-tathbit*), which is the cause of the destruction of those others, just as those others are far from the fragmenting which is the cause of the destruction of these. There is no connection between the two causes, either conceptually or in existence, that would justify one occurring on one side and the other on the other side. Moreover, the agreement of both groups on the general notion of agreement in evil, understood from agreement in a specific evil which is affirmation indicated by dividing, is not useful, since the heading of fragmenting does not indicate that. What indicates it is the dividing of the entrances. Making the relative pronoun a subject, so that its predicate is the oath clause, does not suit the eloquence of the revelation nor the exaltedness of its lofty station. If you know this, then know that the closest of the sayings mentioned is that it is connected to the first, that the dividers are the People of the Two Books, and that the relative pronoun with its clause is a descriptive attribute clarifying the manner of their dividing. The place of the *kaf* (the particle "like") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdariyya*). And the discussion of the exaltedness of the station above comparison is one of the evident insights of noble reflection. The meaning is: "We have indeed given you seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the Great Qur'an, a giving similar to the sending down of the two Books upon their people." The omission of mention of what was sent down to them from the two Books is because the purpose is to explain the similarity between the two givings, not between their objects. The shift from applying what is on the side of the likened-to to what is on the side of the likened, by saying "as We gave the dividers," as occurred in His words, "﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾" and so on, is to draw attention to the distance between the two givings, for the first is by way of honor and favor, and how far apart the two are. This does not detract from its being the likened-to, because that is only on account of its being accepted among them, and the precedence of its existence over the likened in time, not on account of a superiority returning to its essence, as in the Abrahamic prayer, where the likening is not due to God's mercy overflowing upon Abraham and his family being more complete and perfect than what overflowed upon the Prophet, peace be upon him. Rather, that is only due to precedence in existence and explicit mention in the Mighty Qur'an. So there is in the comparison no hint of implying the superiority of the likened-to over the likened, let alone implying the superiority of what the first is connected with over what the second is connected with. They are mentioned under the heading of dividing only to deny that they are characterized by it, although the sending down mentioned negates it, and to announce that it was incumbent upon them to believe in all of it, in accordance with their belief in what was sent down to them, by the ruling of shared cause and unity of reality, which is absolute revelation. The placement of His words, "﴿you shall surely strain﴾," and so on, is for the complete connection with what is intended, the explanation of the state of what was given to the Prophet, peace be upon him. The exaltedness of his rank and the loftiness of his station have been shown first, to such a degree that it calls for his contentment with his station and his sufficiency with it above anything else. Then he was forbidden to turn his attention to the splendor of this world, and the giving of it to its people was expressed as enjoyment, which indicates the imminence of its departure from them. Then grief was expressed over the non-belief of those absorbed in it, while attending to the believers and being content with them rather than others, and by showing his fulfilment of the duties of messengership and the rites of warning, as detailed in the course of what was given to him of the Mighty Qur'an. Then the discussion returned to the manner of his being given, in a way in which was embedded what removes the doubts of the deniers and brings them down from obstinacy, by explaining that he shares with what they have no doubt is true revelation. So reflect: "﴿and with God is the knowledge of the Book﴾." It has also been said: the meaning is, "Say: Indeed I am the clear warner, as We have sent down in the Books that you would come as a warner," and that the dividers are the People of the Book, end of quote. He means that *ma* in *kama* (as) is a relative pronoun. What is meant by the similarity drawn from the *kaf* is agreement, and it, together with what is within its scope, is in the accusative place as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the object of "say": "Say this saying in the state of it being as We sent down upon the People of the Two Books," that is, agreeing with that. Then the most suitable is to interpret the dividing as distortion, so that describing them with that is an allusion to what they did of distortion and concealment of the description of the Prophet, peace be upon him. His words, "﴿fragments﴾" (*'idin*), are the plural of *'iḍa*, which means a group. Its original form is *'iḍwa*, of the pattern *fi'la*, from *'ada al-shah* ("he divided the sheep into limbs") when he made them limbs. It was pluralized with the sound masculine plural to compensate for the omitted letter, like *sinin* and *'izin*. The expression of dividing the Qur'an by *ta'diya*, which is the separating of limbs from a living being that entails the removal of its life and the annulment of its name, rather than mere division or separation, which may exist even in things that do not suffer from being partitioned among the like, is to emphasize the extreme ugliness of what they did to the Mighty Qur'an. It has also been said that it is of the pattern *fi'la* from *'ahahtuhu*, meaning "I slandered him." From Ikrima: *al-'ahh* is sorcery in the language of Quraysh. So its missing letter is a *waw* on the first view and a *ha'* on the second.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 92:

﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ That is: on the Day of Resurrection We will surely question the various categories of the disbelievers, including the ones who divided (the Qur'an), and others, with a question of reproach and rebuke.

"of what they used to do" in the world, by way of speech, action and omission. This includes what has been mentioned of dividing [the Qur'an] and making it into parts (al-taʿdiyah), entering into it in the first instance (dukhūlan awwaliyyan). "And We will surely recompense them for that with a full recompense" (wa-la-najziyannahum bi-dhālika jazāʾan mawfūran). In it there is an intensification and an emphasis of the threat that is not hidden. The fa' (fa-) here indicates the sequencing of the threat upon their deeds, some of which have been mentioned. And in the mention of the attribute of lordship (al-rubūbiyyah), with the pronoun referring to him, peace and blessings be upon him, there is a display of kindness towards him, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾, that is, declare it openly, from "sada'a bi-l-hujjah" (he stated the proof openly) when he speaks it aloud. Or it means "separate the truth from falsehood" (ifraq bayna al-haqq wa-l-batil). Its root meaning is clarification and distinction. The word "ma" (ما) is either a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya) or a relative pronoun (mawsula). The returning pronoun is omitted, so the sense is: what you are commanded with, of the laws deposited within what you were given of the seven oft-repeated (al-mathani al-sab') and the Great Qur'an.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾, that is: do not pay attention to what they say, do not concern yourself with them, and do not seek to take revenge on them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾, by subduing them and destroying them. It is said: they were five of the nobles of Quraysh: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Harith ibn Qays ibn al-Talatila, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib. They went to great lengths in harming the Prophet (ﷺ) and mocking him, so Jibril (upon him be peace) descended and said: "I have been commanded to suffice you against them." He gestured toward the leg of al-Walid, and an arrow passed by and lodged in his garment; he did not bend over to take it out, out of reverence for it, so it struck a vein in his heel and cut it, and he died. He gestured toward the sole of al-'As's foot, and a thorn entered it. He said, "I have been stung, I have been stung," and his leg swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He pointed toward the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he went blind. He pointed toward the nose of al-Harith, and he expelled pus through his nose, and he died. He pointed toward al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth while he was sitting at the base of a tree, and he began striking his head against the tree and hitting his face with its thorns, until he died.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Commentary on Surah 15, verse 96):

﴿Those who set up another god along with Allah﴾: He described them thus to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to make light of the gravity of their conduct toward him, by informing that they did not confine themselves to mocking him, peace and blessings be upon him, but dared to commit the great transgression, which is associating partners with Allah, glorified is He.

﴿But they will come to know﴾ the outcome of what they do and what they neglect.

(p-93) ﴿And indeed We know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾, of the words of polytheism, and of their attacks on the Qur'an and their mockery of it and of you. The emphatic construction of the sentence (tahliyat al-jumla bil-ta'kid) serves to affirm the reality of the consolation it contains; and the use of the present-future form (sighat al-istiqbal) serves to indicate the continuity of the knowledge in accordance with the continuity of its object, namely the continuity of what necessitates it from the statements of the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 15, verse 98:

﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾: Take refuge in God Most High in what distresses you of constriction of the breast and anguish, by glorifying and sanctifying Him, combined with praise of Him. In mentioning the title of lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is evident kindness toward him (ﷺ), and an indication of the reason for the ruling, namely the command to glorify and praise. ﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾, that is, among those who pray, and He will suffice you and remove the grief from you. Or: exalt Him above what they say, combined with praise of Him, for having guided you to the manifest truth. And from him (ﷺ) it is related that: "Whenever a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer."

﴿And worship your Lord﴾: persist in the worship of Him, exalted is He, in which you are already engaged. The use of the explicit mention with the title that preceded it a moment ago serves to confirm the kindness previously shown to him, upon him be prayers and peace, and to indicate the reason for the command to worship.

﴿until there comes to you the certainty﴾: that is, death, for it is certain to overtake every living creature. Attributing the coming to it is to inform that it is directed toward the living and seeks to reach him. The meaning is: persist in worship for as long as you are alive, without neglecting it for a moment.

On the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Hijr will have ten good deeds recorded for him, equal in number to the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), and those who mocked Muhammad (ﷺ)."
